💡 Key Takeaways
  • In a recent development, this is a human-written story voiced by AI.
  • The walnut-sized fear center of the brain also distinguishes the memorable from the mundane.
  • Neurons in the amygdala act like a save button for memories, scientists report October 27 in Nature Neuroscience.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In a recent development, this is a human-written story voiced by AI. Got feedback? Take our survey . (See our AI policy here .).

The walnut-sized fear center of the brain also distinguishes the memorable from the mundane.

Neurons in the amygdala act like a save button for memories, scientists report October 27 in Nature Neuroscience. Though the study doesn’t nail down the exact mechanism for memory formation, it points to a broader role for the amygdala within the memory-sorting apparatus.

It has been revealed that the study probes an enduring quandary about the mind, says neuroscientist Jiayang Xiao of Cedars-Sinai Health Sciences University in Los Angeles. “We forget much of what we experience … only a fraction of the information we encounter becomes a lasting memory,” she says.

It has been revealed that although a role for the amygdala in memory has been suggested before, previous studies that used electrodes reading brain activity through the scalp, or at the scale of thousands rather than individual neurons, captured a blurrier picture. It’s akin to a microphone recording from outside of a stadium, says cognitive neuroscientist Cory Inman at the University of Utah in Salt Lake City, who was not involved in the study.

According to recent reports, “You might be able to tell that there’s a game happening. You might be able to tell when somebody scores a touchdown. You might even be able to tell that one side of the stadium is cheering for one team and another side of the stadium is cheering for another team,” but that’s about it, Inman says. The fresh study is more like a lapel mic pinned on a single fan in terms of scale and what the researchers were able to capture, adding clarity.

The amygdala, which is typically associated with regulating emotions like fear and aggression, has neurons that are challenging to reach, residing in two clusters deep within the brain. Xiao and her colleagues leveraged electrodes previously surgically implanted in more than 90 people with drug-resistant epilepsy to identify where seizures originate. In their fresh role, the electrodes singled out neurons involved in saving memories.

Sources indicate that patients were shown images of everyday objects belonging to five categories such as food and animals. About 10 to 30 minutes later, they attempted to recall which images were already shown. Xiao and her colleagues found that activity in certain amygdala neurons corresponded with an image being remembered. The image had been earmarked for longer term storage, Xiao says.

It has been revealed that although participants had to recall something from half an hour ago at most and the exact mechanism for saving memories is still unclear, the researchers think there are two main steps of the process. The team showed that individual neurons have a preference for one of the five categories of images. First the image is categorized by the amygdala. Then, the strength of the category neuron response the first time the image is shown dictates whether the image is later recalled.

A better understanding of this mechanism may pave the way for more effective treatments of memory disorders, Xiao indicates, a medical conundrum for which there are at the moment no broadly effective treatments.

Sources indicate that the hippocampus is typically more directly linked to memory, so “it surprised me that we observe such a clear relationship between memory formation and activity in the amygdala,” Xiao says. By contrast, the correlation between hippocampus neuron activity and image recall was weaker and slightly delayed.

Future work like observing the impacts of stimulating amygdala neurons on memory will help researchers discern if this region can be targeted to improve memory, Xiao says.

For now, the secret to memory’s hidden machinations remains in the shadows.

Latest Update: Heart Stents May Not Prevent Heart Attacks or Early Death, Landmark Study Finds

📅 20 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (745 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Scitechdaily

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • A stent can restore blood flow to the heart, but in people with stable coronary disease, it may offer no added protection against heart attacks or early death.
  • For someone told they have a narrowed heart artery, opening it can seem like the obvious next step.
  • According to recent reports, researchers led by Neel Butala, MD, of the University of Colorado Anschutz, examined that question through an extended follow-up of participants in the COURAGE trial.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

A stent can restore blood flow to the heart, but in people with stable coronary disease, it may offer no added protection against heart attacks or early death.

For someone told they have a narrowed heart artery, opening it can seem like the obvious next step. Yet improving blood flow and preventing future health problems are separate goals, and a procedure that achieves one may not necessarily achieve the other.

According to recent reports, researchers led by Neel Butala, MD, of the University of Colorado Anschutz, examined that question through an extended follow-up of participants in the COURAGE trial. They found no statistically significant difference in the combined risk of death or heart attack between patients initially assigned to an artery-opening procedure plus medical therapy and those assigned to medical therapy alone.

Published in JAMA and presented at the 2026 American Heart Association Scientific Sessions, the findings offer an unusually long look at how these treatment strategies compare.

The original COURAGE trial enrolled people with stable coronary artery disease and compared optimal medical therapy alone with optimal medical therapy plus percutaneous coronary intervention (PCI), commonly known as angioplasty.

In a recent development, during angioplasty, doctors inflate a small balloon inside a narrowed artery to improve blood flow. They often place a tiny metal tube called a stent to help keep the artery open.

For the newly introduced analysis, researchers tracked 959 participants through linked health records. The median follow-up was 15 years, with some patients followed for as long as 25 years. The estimated 25-year cumulative incidence of death or heart attack was 93.3% in the group initially assigned to PCI plus medical therapy and 91% in the medical therapy group. That difference was not statistically significant.

Industry observers note that earlier research had examined long-term survival after the trial. This analysis also included heart attacks, allowing researchers to assess whether an initial PCI strategy might prevent cardiovascular events that would not be captured by survival figures alone.

Industry observers note that the central finding concerns what happens after an artery has been successfully opened. Restoring blood flow can relieve symptoms, but the study did not find evidence that starting with PCI lowered the combined long-term risk of heart attack or death.

Recent findings suggest that “When we open a blocked artery, we know we’ve improved blood flow through that artery, and that relieves symptoms. But the bigger question is whether that translates into a reduction in clinical events such as heart attacks or death for patients over the long term. That’s what we wanted to understand with this study,” said Butala, an assistant professor of medicine-cardiology at the CU Anschutz School of Medicine.

“We found no significant difference in the risk of death or heart attack between the two treatment groups. That’s important information for doctors and patients as they consider the best approach to treating stable coronary artery disease.”.

These results do not mean angioplasty and stents are unnecessary. They can relieve chest pain and other symptoms, while emergency procedures can be lifesaving during certain types of heart attacks. The study specifically examined an initial PCI strategy for stable coronary disease, so its findings should be understood within that setting.

Industry observers note that although the participants came from a randomized trial, this analysis was a post hoc observational follow-up, rather than a latest randomized trial. It included veterans whose health records could be linked, a group with higher baseline health risks than the full COURAGE trial population.

In a recent development, the researchers also acknowledged limitations in identifying heart attacks through routinely collected health records. However, the findings were consistent with events independently verified during the original trial.

It has been revealed that the research helps clarify what an initial procedure may accomplish. Symptom relief remains a meaningful benefit, but the long-term findings do not establish additional protection against heart attack or death compared with medical therapy alone. Butala said considering both immediate relief and future health outcomes can support more informed treatment decisions.

Recent findings suggest that reference: “Percutaneous Coronary Intervention and Long-Term Outcomes in Stable Coronary Artery Disease: Extended Follow-Up of the COURAGE Randomized Trial” by Neel M. Butala, Nandini Murali, Natalia Rahman, Shayna Cave, Siamack Ayandeh, Mary E. Plomondon, Jonathan W. Cunningham, William S. Weintraub, Robert W. Yeh, Stephen W. Waldo and William E. Boden, 7 November 2026, JAMA. DOI: 10.1001/jama.2026.23488.

The Forever Chemicals Wreaking Havoc on Our Planet Are About to Meet Their Kryptonite

📅 20 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 3 min read (532 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Popularmechanics

⏱️ ~3 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • One of the most worrisome side effects of modern life is a class of chemicals called per- and polyfluoroalkyl substances, or PFAS.
  • Today, nearly all humans, including newborns, have detectable levels of PFAS in their blood.
  • One promising approach to combating PFAS is to find a way to break their super-strong chemical bonds, then bake that chemistry into next-generation filters.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

One of the most worrisome side effects of modern life is a class of chemicals called per- and polyfluoroalkyl substances, or PFAS. These man-made compounds show up in everything from non-stick pans to fast-food wrappers. They’re called “forever chemicals” because their carbon-fluorine bonds are so strong that they barely break down. The PFAS family includes nearly 15,000 different compounds, according to the U.S. Environmental Protection Agency, but the FDA tests food and animal feed for only a couple dozen of them.

Today, nearly all humans, including newborns, have detectable levels of PFAS in their blood.

One promising approach to combating PFAS is to find a way to break their super-strong chemical bonds, then bake that chemistry into next-generation filters. Currently, filters can trap a variety of PFAS but can’t destroy them, meaning the filters basically just move the toxic chemicals from one place to another. However, a study in the journal Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences describes a filter that uses hydrogen to attack carbon-fluorine bonds. When tested against six PFAS of regulatory concern, it worked on all of them.

Recent findings suggest that “PFAS are hard to break down, and normal processes that we use don’t work,” Arizona State University’s Bruce Rittmann, the senior author of the study, mentioned in a press statement. “We demonstrated that this mechanism worked for all six. It’s a universal mechanism.”.

Hydrogen is essential for this process because once activated into a reactive form, it drives a process known as “hydrodefluorination,” stripping and replacing the fluorine and forming carbon-hydrogen bonds. To activate that hydrogen, Rittman and his team used palladium nanoparticles that can convert the hydrogen gas into its much-needed reactive form.

“The palladium attracts the PFAS molecule, and the palladium attracts the hydrogen and puts them together,” Rittmann mentioned in a press statement.

Recent findings suggest that as hydrogen and PFAS travel through the membrane, both are attracted to the palladium catalyst. However, hydrogen isn’t simply added to the waste stream—instead, it’s fed directly into the membrane itself. This gives the filter the perfect opportunity to chemically dismantle those troublesome carbon-fluorine bonds. Over two months of continuous operation, the membrane broke apart most of the PFAS it captured. It removed 90 percent of the chemicals and stripped about 83 percent of their fluorine.

Recent findings suggest that that’s a huge advancement for combating the proliferation of PFAS in the natural environment, but a big limitation will be cost. Simply put, palladium isn’t cheap, and Rittman estimates that roughly a kilogram of the stuff costs about $50,000. The new approach could be paired with conventional treatments, which would first concentrate the PFAS into a smaller waste stream that the palladium membrane could then destroy.

“Decades of extensive deployment of PFAS in firefighting foams, oil- and water-repellent surfaces, non-stick cookware, and food-contact materials have created diffuse, chronic inputs into watersheds and drinking-water supplies,” the authors wrote in the study. “Hydrogen-driven hydrodefluorination offers a direct reductive route under comparatively mild conditions.”.

Alzheimer’s Breakthrough: Researchers Find Fresh Clues to Cognitive Decline in Healthy Adults

📅 20 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 3 min read (696 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Scitechdaily

⏱️ ~3 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Researchers have identified a promising way to assess Alzheimer’s-related cognitive risks in otherwise healthy older adults.
  • In a recent development, A blood test could help estimate whether someone with no memory problems will develop cognitive impairment within the next five or 10 years.
  • For example, a 75-year-old woman without the APOE e4 genetic risk variant had an estimated five-year risk of mild cognitive impairment (MCI) of 5% when her biomarker level was relatively low.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Researchers have identified a promising way to assess Alzheimer’s-related cognitive risks in otherwise healthy older adults.

In a recent development, A blood test could help estimate whether someone with no memory problems will develop cognitive impairment within the next five or 10 years. In a newly introduced Mayo Clinic study published in JAMA Neurology, researchers developed a method that combines an Alzheimer’s-related blood biomarker with age, sex, and genetic risk to produce personalized estimates.

For example, a 75-year-old woman without the APOE e4 genetic risk variant had an estimated five-year risk of mild cognitive impairment (MCI) of 5% when her biomarker level was relatively low. At a higher level, that estimate rose to 16%. Her predicted 10-year risk increased from 12% to 35%.

In a recent development, the method measures phosphorylated Tau 217 (p-tau217), a protein associated with Alzheimer’s disease. Elevated levels in the blood are linked to Alzheimer’s-related changes in the brain, but a positive biomarker result alone cannot determine whether or when someone will develop cognitive symptoms.

“The goal is to provide a personalized estimate of the risk of developing cognitive impairment that is more meaningful than simply reporting whether a blood test is positive or negative for amyloid pathology,” indicates Alicia Algeciras-Schimnich, Ph.D., a Mayo Clinic laboratory medicine and pathology researcher and first author of the study.

The research builds on an earlier Mayo Clinic prediction model that used positron emission tomography (PET) brain scans to detect amyloid, a protein that accumulates in the brains of people with Alzheimer’s disease. Measuring p-tau217 in blood offers a less invasive approach that could be used more widely.

Researchers analyzed data from 1,644 cognitively healthy participants in the Mayo Clinic Study of Aging and 534 participants in the Alzheimer’s Disease Neuroimaging Initiative. All were between 60 and 90 years old and had undergone blood biomarker measurements, genetic testing, and repeated cognitive assessments.

Using the Mayo Clinic data, the team calculated the probability of developing MCI or dementia within five or 10 years. Higher p-tau217 levels and older age were associated with greater risk. At the same elevated biomarker level, the estimated five-year risk of MCI was 6% for a 65-year-old but 37% for an 85-year-old.

The researchers then examined the Alzheimer’s Disease Neuroimaging Initiative data, which independently supported the association between elevated p-tau217 and increased risk of cognitive decline.

In a recent development, the approach could eventually help doctors identify people who might benefit from preventive treatment before memory problems begin. However, its clinical usefulness will depend partly on whether therapies can successfully delay cognitive decline in people who have no symptoms.

It has been revealed that “A person may want to know: What is my risk of developing cognitive impairment in the next five or 10 years, and how does this blood test change that risk?” claims Ronald Petersen, M.D., Ph.D., a Mayo Clinic neurologist and director of the Mayo Clinic Study of Aging. “If preventive therapies prove effective, those numbers could become very notable in treatment decisions.”.

In a recent development, clinical trials, including AHEAD 3-45 and TRAILBLAZER-ALZ 3, are investigating whether treatments targeting amyloid can delay cognitive decline before symptoms develop. Both trials have used blood biomarkers to help identify participants, highlighting their potential role in earlier Alzheimer’s research.

“Absolute risk gives the biomarker result clinical context,” says Clifford Jack Jr., M.D., a Mayo Clinic neuroradiologist and senior author of the study. “If preventive treatments become available, this kind of information could help patients and clinicians have more informed conversations about the potential benefits and risks of treatment.”.

The risk estimates were developed using the Mayo Clinic Study of Aging and require further evaluation in more diverse populations and with other p-tau217 blood tests. Although the findings support the potential of personalized risk prediction, Alzheimer’s biomarker testing is not currently recommended for people without cognitive symptoms.

Sources indicate that reference: “Absolute Risk of Progression to Cognitive Impairment Based on Plasma Phosphorylated Tau 217, Age, Sex, and APOE ε4” by Alicia Algeciras-Schimnich, Mingzhao Hu, Stephen D. Weigand, et al., 16 November 2026, JAMA Neurology. DOI: 10.1001/jamaneurol.2026.4292.

#42917. Scientists Develop New Nanomaterial That Could Help the Body Regrow Missing Bone

General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Scitechdaily ↗ Open Full Page

Scientists Develop New Nanomaterial That Could Help the Body Regrow Missing Bone

📅 20 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (891 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Scitechdaily

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • A biodegradable material developed by Australian researchers could eventually help children born with cleft lip and palate regrow missing jawbone without undergoing invasive bone graft surgery.
  • Developed at the University of Sydney in collaboration with the University of Queensland, the material works by activating the body’s existing repair signals rather than supplying external growth factors.
  • Industry observers note that cleft lip and palate affects approximately one in 700 children and develops when parts of the upper lip or roof of the mouth fail to fuse completely during pregnancy.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

A biodegradable material developed by Australian researchers could eventually help children born with cleft lip and palate regrow missing jawbone without undergoing invasive bone graft surgery. In preclinical testing, the experimental nanomaterial produced approximately 80 percent more new bone than a control material after eight weeks.

Developed at the University of Sydney in collaboration with the University of Queensland, the material works by activating the body’s existing repair signals rather than supplying external growth factors. Researchers hope the approach could eventually allow children to receive treatment years earlier than is typically possible today.

Industry observers note that cleft lip and palate affects approximately one in 700 children and develops when parts of the upper lip or roof of the mouth fail to fuse completely during pregnancy. Correcting the resulting jawbone defects is among the most challenging aspects of treatment, with potential consequences for eating, breathing, speech, and social development.

“One of the biggest challenges for children born with cleft lip and palate is repairing the bone defect in the jaw,” remarked lead researcher Associate Professor Chun Xu, a Sydney Horizon Fellow in the University of Sydney’s Faculty of Medicine and Health.

“While some children with minor defects are treated as infants, many patients need to wait until they are around 10 to 12 years old before surgeons can take bone from another part of the body and graft it into the defect.

It has been revealed that “That means many kids live with difficulties for years. It can affect their breathing, eating and speech. Most heartbreaking of all, it can have a huge impact on their confidence and social development.”.

According to recent reports, more than four million bone repair procedures are performed worldwide annually. Many current treatments rely on bone harvested from the patient or animal-derived materials that primarily provide structural support. The fresh approach instead aims to stimulate the formation of living bone using a biodegradable calcium-aluminosilicate nanomaterial.

The material activates a naturally occurring growth factor called latent Transforming Growth Factor β1 (TGF-β1). This protein normally exists in an inactive form until biological signals trigger its activity. Once activated, it helps recruit stem cells to the damaged area and encourages their development into bone-producing cells. As latest tissue forms, the biodegradable material is gradually replaced by the patient’s own bone.

“The material activates dormant repair signals in the body, triggering a cascade of healing processes that attract bone-forming stem cells and stimulate fresh bone growth,” Xu explained.

“Our body already contains many of the signals needed for tissue repair,” Associate Professor Xu mentioned.

According to recent reports, “We’ve developed a material that can help activate those signals at the right place and time. Instead of supplying external growth factors, we’re encouraging the body to use its own healing potential.”.

According to recent reports, the study, published in ACS Nano, found that the material activated the body’s latent bone repair growth factor at approximately 10 times the level achieved using conventional methods. It also promoted blood clotting within about 30 seconds, which could help stabilize an injury during the earliest stages of healing.

Sources indicate that according to the researchers, this is the first demonstration of a single nanomaterial platform capable of combining rapid blood clotting, activation of naturally occurring growth factors, recruitment of bone-forming stem cells, and enhanced bone regeneration. The findings come from a preclinical bone model, however, and further testing is necessary to determine whether the material can be used safely and effectively in humans.

Xu and his colleagues envision a future in which bone defects can be repaired earlier in childhood, potentially reducing the need to remove healthy bone from elsewhere in the body.

“Our long-term goal is to develop materials that help the body regenerate bone naturally and reduce the need for these invasive and painful procedures. We hope this could allow treatment much earlier than is possible today.”.

The researchers are also investigating whether the nanomaterial could be incorporated into personalized 3D-printed scaffolds designed to fit an individual’s bone defect. Beyond cleft lip and palate, potential applications include repairing bone damaged by traumatic injuries, tooth loss, and other conditions involving difficult-to-heal defects.

“Every patient is different, and every bone defect is different,” Xu said.

“In the future, we hope to combine these materials with advanced 3D-printing technologies so treatments can be tailored to the specific needs of each patient.”.

The technology remains at the preclinical stage, with additional research required before human trials can begin.

According to recent reports, reference: “Multifunctional Mesoporous Calcium-Aluminosilicate Nanoparticles Enable Heterogeneous Activation of Endogenous Transforming Growth Factor β1 and Rapid Hemostasis for Bone Repair” by Chun Xu, Qingxuan Chen, Hang Chen, Aoni Xu, Juan Wen, Yiwei Li, Huan Dai, Siyuan Liu, Dan Cheng, Yaping Song, Bing Sun, Jie Tang, Jie Fan, Chang Lei and Chengzhong Yu, 15 September 2026, ACS Nano. DOI: 10.1021/acsnano.6c05126.

The authors acknowledge the funding support from Australian Research Council, National Health and Medical Research Council and the University of Sydney. A provisional patent application related to the findings reported in this manuscript has been filed by the University of Sydney and the University of Queensland. The application covers calcium-aluminosilicate mesoporous nanoparticles and their use for bone repair, as described in the paper (Provisional Patent Application No. 2026903515).

An Ancient Coffin in a Famous Church Held the Wrong Body for 1,000 Years. Now We May Know Who’s Inside.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Recent findings suggest that for more than 150 years, a burial found on the grounds of Westminster Abbey remained a mystery.
  • According to recent reports, if you went only by the inscription carved on the limestone sarcophagus excavated on the North Green at Westminster Abbey in 1869, you’d understandably assume it held the remains of Valerius Amandinus, a wealthy Briton who lived in Roman Britain around 300 C.E.
  • It certainly didn’t help that a written account in 1873 declared the skeleton lost.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Recent findings suggest that for more than 150 years, a burial found on the grounds of Westminster Abbey remained a mystery. Clues from the coffin itself, not to mention the skeleton inside, puzzled experts until Westminster Abbey’s consultant archaeologist, Warwick Rodwell, identified the deceased as a high-ranking medieval monk. He went one step further, determining the bones belonged to Aelfwig, an abbot of the Abbey’s Benedictine monastery, although Rodwell left open the possibility that the occupant was another abbot.

According to recent reports, if you went only by the inscription carved on the limestone sarcophagus excavated on the North Green at Westminster Abbey in 1869, you’d understandably assume it held the remains of Valerius Amandinus, a wealthy Briton who lived in Roman Britain around 300 C.E. Archaeological research isn’t that simple, though. A Latin cross dated to the 10th or 11th century was also carved across the lid, likely when the coffin was reused, so with conflicting symbology muddying the waters, the identity of the person entombed on the Abbey’s grounds remained unknown for generations.

It certainly didn’t help that a written account in 1873 declared the skeleton lost. In 2016, however, conservators found the bones where they had presumably been all along: inside the coffin.

Rodwell worked on the puzzle for years, eventually publishing a study in the Journal of the British Archaeological Association explaining how the evidence led him to two abbots who served at the monastery. His first candidate, Aelfwig, died around 1020, but the second option was Aelfwig’s successor, Wulfnoth, who died 29 years later.

It has been revealed that “We have two viable contenders for the occupant of the sarcophagus,” Rodwell stated in a statement from the Abbey. He ruled out Aelfwig’s predecessor because that abbot left the area and died elsewhere. “We do not know the date of birth of either. But either would fit equally well if we assume the abbot was in his early 20s when the appointment was made and close to 50 when he died. The fact Aelfwig was already a monk of Westminster might favor him.”.

It has been revealed that the sarcophagus’s own history reveals little. The limestone probably came from Oxfordshire, England. But Rodwell wrote that no clues link the sarcophagus to its original burial site or explain why it was later moved, even though the inscription clearly ties it to a Briton who lived about 1,700 years ago. Identification is further complicated by the Anglo-Saxon cross added to the lid centuries later and by Rodwell’s belief that grave goods were stolen in the early 19th century.

It has been revealed that to learn more about the man himself, Rodwell worked with James Young Langhorne, a human bone specialist from Pre-Construct Archaeology. They determined that the man was between 35 and 49 years old and stood about 5 feet, 9 inches tall. That contradicts the 19th-century assessment, which described him as a “robust young man” no older than 30 and about 5 feet, 7 inches tall. The analysis also highlighted osteoarthritis in multiple joints, two healed rib fractures, and signs of an old infection in one leg. There was no obvious cause of death.

Sources indicate that radiocarbon dating by the Scottish Universities Environmental Research Centre placed the bones between 987 and 1052 C.E. This confirmed that the sarcophagus had been reused, and the date range matches the Saxon-period cross on the lid. With that range established, Rodwell looked more closely at the possible candidates.

He concluded the man was an abbot because he was “honored” with burial in a “fine sarcophagus”: his wooden coffin was packed in lime and placed inside the stone casket. To support his theory further, Rodwell wrote that he believes the “prestigious burial” first took place in the eastern arm of the abbey church. The sarcophagus would have been fully buried, with the recut lid serving as a cross-slab in the church floor. Then, after Henry III began rebuilding the abbey in the 1240s, workers moved the sarcophagus into the “newly constructed sacristy courtyard” in 1258.

Today, the sarcophagus is on permanent display in the Abbey’s museum, The Queen’s Diamond Jubilee Galleries.

Tim Newcomb is a journalist based in the Pacific Northwest. He covers stadiums, sneakers, gear, infrastructure, and more for a variety of publications, including Popular Mechanics. His favorite interviews have included sit-downs with Roger Federer in Switzerland, Kobe Bryant in Los Angeles, and Tinker Hatfield in Portland.

Industry News: The ‘hell chicken’ dinosaur was a real terror — to fruit

💡 Key Takeaways
  • It has been revealed that this is a human-written story voiced by AI.
  • Sources indicate that more than 65 million years ago, a small, beaked dinosaur dubbed the “hell chicken” was a real terror – to fruit.
  • It’s the first evidence of non-avian dinosaurs evolving specialized adaptations for eating fruit, and comes at a time when flowering plants were coming into their own, researchers report October 10 in Nature Communications.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It has been revealed that this is a human-written story voiced by AI. Got feedback? Take our survey . (See our AI policy here .).

Sources indicate that more than 65 million years ago, a small, beaked dinosaur dubbed the “hell chicken” was a real terror – to fruit. Reconstruction of its beak and jaw suggest it mashed up fruit much like modern parrots.

It’s the first evidence of non-avian dinosaurs evolving specialized adaptations for eating fruit, and comes at a time when flowering plants were coming into their own, researchers report October 10 in Nature Communications.

Recent findings suggest that in 2011, a fossil collector found much of the fossilized skeleton of an odd theropod dinosaur in eastern Montana and brought to the attention of David Evans, a paleontologist at the Royal Ontario Museum in Canada. Over the next several years, fossil collectors and paleontologists working in Montana and North and South Dakota unearthed four more partial skeletons.

Sources indicate that the dinosaur belonged to a particularly birdlike subgroup of beaked theropods called oviraptorosaurs that lived during the Cretaceous Period. This species probably weighed around 12 kilograms — about the size of a turkey.

Evans and Greg Funston — a paleontologist at Stony Brook University in Upcoming York — and their colleagues named it Infernogallus jamesi, or ‘hell chicken,’ after its discovery in the Hell Creek geological formation and its overall poultrylike appearance.

When the researchers studied Infernogallus’s skull and reconstructed the musculature, they discovered that it was no ordinary theropod. The construction of its jaw joints, muscles and palate suggest that it moved its jaw forward and back when eating rather than up and down like its chomping relatives.

This chewing style is unique among non-avian dinosaurs but is strikingly similar to that of fruit-eating parrots. Funston and his colleagues think Infernogallus had adapted to a fruit-rich diet, deftly stripping the flesh from large seeds using its tongue and sliding jaw motions.

These fruit-munching adaptations were surprising, Funston indicates. “But the more we delved into it, the more sense it made,” he says. “All the different lines of evidence seemed to converge on this one answer.”.

According to recent reports, angiosperms — plants that produce flowers and fruits — were rapidly diversifying throughout the Cretaceous. Mounting evidence suggests that angiosperms were coevolving with Cretaceous animals, and that dinosaurs may have been eating their fruits. Infernogallus adds to that emerging picture. It’s possible that other ‘hell chicken’ relatives or other dinosaur groups were habitual fruit eaters too, Funston claims.

“[The discovery] suggests that our picture of dinosaur ecology right before the Cretaceous extinction has been missing major puzzle pieces, and that dinosaurs were more diverse than we thought.”.

Does the Sun Have a Secret Companion? A Controversial Theory Could Explain Earth’s Mass Extinctions

📅 20 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (931 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Scitechdaily

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • A mysterious 26-million-year pattern in Earth’s extinction history has fueled a controversial theory involving an unseen stellar companion to the Sun.
  • Scientists have long believed that long-period comets with highly inclined orbits, some capable of causing mass extinctions on Earth, originate in the hypothetical Oort Cloud.
  • Richard Muller, a well-known professor emeritus of physics at the University of California, Berkeley, has proposed another explanation for why some of these comets enter the inner solar system.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

A mysterious 26-million-year pattern in Earth’s extinction history has fueled a controversial theory involving an unseen stellar companion to the Sun.

Scientists have long believed that long-period comets with highly inclined orbits, some capable of causing mass extinctions on Earth, originate in the hypothetical Oort Cloud. This vast, roughly spherical reservoir of icy bodies is thought to contain trillions of objects and extend as far as 1.6 light-years from the Sun.

Richard Muller, a well-known professor emeritus of physics at the University of California, Berkeley, has proposed another explanation for why some of these comets enter the inner solar system. In addition to gravitational disturbances caused by passing stars, he suggests that a low-mass red dwarf star (dubbed Nemesis) could periodically redirect comets toward the Sun. Under this hypothesis, Nemesis and the Sun orbit a shared center of gravity.

According to Muller, Nemesis follows a slightly elongated orbit that periodically brings it into regions of the Oort Cloud, where its gravity could disrupt the paths of billions of comets.

Muller explained in a phone interview that these encounters could trigger comet showers lasting roughly a million years. The greatest number of comets would be redirected into the inner solar system when Nemesis passes through the cloud’s densest regions.

The proposed Nemesis star is not related to the hypothetical Planet X. It also differs from unrelated stars that occasionally pass near the solar system and gravitationally disturb the Oort Cloud, potentially sending numerous comets inward.

According to recent reports, unlike these unpredictable stellar encounters, the Nemesis hypothesis proposes a recurring cycle. Muller believes this mechanism could explain a pattern of impacts on Earth spanning approximately 250 million years.

According to recent reports, muller points to a 1982 study published in the journal Science by paleontologists David Raup and Jack Sepkoski. The researchers compiled an extensive record of marine extinctions that, according to Muller, revealed a striking pattern of extinction events occurring roughly every 26 million years.

The challenge was to come up with an explanation, claims Muller. “Well, maybe there’s a companion star that comes close in to the Oort Cloud every 26 million years, and then triggers a comet hitting Earth,” he says.

It’s an idea that Muller still very much supports, although he isn’t sanguine about being able to directly observe Nemesis.

Despite what others seem to think, there is no clear evidence against this hypothesis, notes Muller.

The Oort Cloud, a heretofore unseen, largely spherical cloud of comets and small icy bodies left over from the formation of our solar system some 4.5 billion years ago, very much remains a mystery.

There are three sources for the original material that formed the Oort Cloud, Astrophysicist Sean Raymond, Director of France’s Bordeaux Astrophysical Laboratory, told me via email.

Planetesimals that originated in our Sun’s planet-forming disk; planetesimals that originated around other stars in our Sun’s birth cluster, and interstellar objects that were captured during stellar encounters or by scattering by Jupiter, he notes.

According to recent reports, many astronomers assume that if Nemesis is an ordinary red dwarf, somebody would have seen it, and the answer is no, because it’s moving with the Sun around the center of gravity. And as a result, Nemesis doesn’t show enough proper motion, or movement across our line of sight, to be detectable.

But it must be substantial enough to perturb the Oort cloud, which means it’s probably at least five percent the mass of the Sun, says Muller.

The consensus view is the K-T extinction event, which impacted the Yucatan Peninsula some 66 million years ago, was most likely caused by a large asteroid.

It has been revealed that yet the evidence that it’s an asteroid rather than a comet is very weak, so people say asteroid because that’s what Walter Alvarez, a professor of Earth and Planetary Science also at the University of California, Berkeley, said in his initial K-T Boundary paper, Muller notes. But when I asked Alvarez, I said, “You said asteroid. Could it be a comet?”.

He responded, “Sure, we couldn’t tell the difference.”.

The best near-term chance of characterizing this massive cloud, however, comes from the Rubin Observatory, which is just coming online. Astronomers hope that Rubin will be able to detect more long-period Oort Cloud comets.

The next comet shower that could cause serious damage to Earth should not be for another 12 to 15 million years from now, claims Muller.

The bad news is that if it’s out there, Nemesis almost certainly would lie close to the plane of the ecliptic, which means that from our point of view, it would lie coplanar with most of the bodies of the outer solar system. And as a dim 8th or possibly 9th magnitude star, this would make it even more difficult to spot, certainly impossible to see with the naked eye.

So, Nemesis really is probably lost in a field of view that includes a huge number of other stars, claims Muller.

References: “Dynamical Population of Comet Reservoirs” by Nathan A. Kaib and Kathryn Volk, May 30, 2022, arXiv. DOI: 2206.00010.

In a recent development, “Measurement of the lunar impact record for the past 3.5 b.y. and implications for the Nemesis theory” by Richard A. Muller, 01 January 2002, Geological Society of America DOI: 10.1130/0-8137-2356-6.659.

In a recent development, “Mass Extinctions in the Marine Fossil Record” by David M. Raup and J. John Sepkoski, Jr., 19 March 1982, Science. DOI: 10.1126/science.215.4539.1501.

Latest Update: You Can Build All the Power Plants You Want. Without This Overlooked Machine, None of Them Will Matter.

📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • As humanity entered the 21st century and the ravages of climate change became more and more apparent, the push toward electrification (replacing gas-powered cars, furnaces, and stoves with electric versions) really gained steam.
  • But building out an electrified future isn’t as easy as sticking wind turbines in the ocean and vast solar arrays in the desert and calling it a day.
  • In a upcoming study published in the journal Cell Reports Sustainability, researchers at Johns Hopkins University report that critical grid equipment, such as transformers and converters, could become the bottleneck in powering a rapidly electrifying society.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

As humanity entered the 21st century and the ravages of climate change became more and more apparent, the push toward electrification (replacing gas-powered cars, furnaces, and stoves with electric versions) really gained steam. At the same time, the electricity supply itself has been getting cleaner. According to Pew Research, solar power accounted for only 0.01 percent of the world’s electricity production back then, but fast-forward a quarter of a century, and that number is now nine percent and rising.

But building out an electrified future isn’t as easy as sticking wind turbines in the ocean and vast solar arrays in the desert and calling it a day. These new forms of renewable energy also need to connect to the grid before they can supply us with that much-needed new power. Expanding the grid’s capacity to meet this ballooning demand was already going to be a tall order as more and more electric cars, ovens, and heat pumps came online. Now, the rise of power-hungry AI data centers has transformed that difficult task into a borderline impossible one for the simple reason that the U.S. may not have enough of the equipment—or the materials to make said equipment—to build the required infrastructure.

In a upcoming study published in the journal Cell Reports Sustainability, researchers at Johns Hopkins University report that critical grid equipment, such as transformers and converters, could become the bottleneck in powering a rapidly electrifying society. According to the researchers, demand for electricity isn’t anything new. In fact, it’s been steadily rising since Thomas Edison flipped the switch on the Pearl Street Station in 1882. But due to the rise of AI data centers, the electricity industry has entered a whole new era of demand growth.

Industry observers note that “When the demand for electricity started to grow faster than expected, it started to amplify all the cracks in the industry,” Yury Dvorkin, a Johns Hopkins researcher and co-author of the study, mentioned in a press statement. According to Dvorkin and co-author Boyu Yao, electricity demand historically ticked up a percent or two each year. But now, largely because of data centers, demand is projected to grow 21 percent overall by the end of the decade.

If this rapid demand growth persists, it will put considerable strain on supplies of specific materials, including copper, steel, nickel, aluminum, and manganese, needed to build the necessary transformers, which step up or step down the voltage of alternating current on the grid.

“This type of equipment was taken for granted, but without it, you can build a data center or a power plant but it won’t be powered because you cannot connect it to the grid,” Dvorkin noted. “By 2030 we’re likely to have transformer shortages even without the most aggressive power demand growth.”.

Recent findings suggest that according to their projections, copper will run short in 2027, followed soon by steel and nickel, which will affect not just grid utilities but wind power infrastructure and electric vehicle charging stations. This shortfall isn’t necessarily news: a study by S&P Global earlier this year found that copper could experience a 10 million metric ton deficit by 2040. This deficit isn’t caused by a lack of copper in the ground, since the planet holds abundant copper resources. Extraction is where the industry is facing a crucial bottleneck.

“Copper is abundant in the ground, but there’s not enough being extracted to be able to meet the demand,” authors of a copper market analysis wrote for The Conversation earlier this year. That’s because investors want higher and more reliable returns than copper mines right now offer, and the industry faces complex permitting processes and can’t find enough workers.

Sources indicate that this new study suggests that under its baseline scenario, the U.S. might be able to produce enough transformers yet still fall 16 percent short on other grid-related equipment. But with AI data centers supercharging demand, the study’s “high power demand” scenario is more likely. That scenario projects a 15 percent shortage of transformers and a 30 percent shortage of all other equipment. The authors also note that roughly two-thirds of this expected shortage can be attributed to AI data centers.

“Utilities will compete for transformers with the data center industry,” Dvorkin noted. “Transformers will first be delivered to whoever can pay the highest premium. Will it be a mom-and-pop utility or a massive data center corporation?”.

I think we already know the answer to that question.

Breaking: NASA Smashed Into an Asteroid. Now ESA’s Hera Spacecraft Is About to Reveal the Damage

📅 21 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (945 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Scitechdaily

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Sources indicate that the European Space Agency’s (ESA) Hera spacecraft has reached the two asteroids it was sent to investigate, marking a major milestone in a mission designed to strengthen Earth’s defenses against dangerous space rocks.
  • It has been revealed that the spacecraft has entered its initial observation period, known as the ‘early characterization phase’.
  • “Our aim right now is to gather the major-picture findings of relevance to supporting the mission’s planetary defense goals,” explains mission scientist Michael Kueppers.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Sources indicate that the European Space Agency’s (ESA) Hera spacecraft has reached the two asteroids it was sent to investigate, marking a major milestone in a mission designed to strengthen Earth’s defenses against dangerous space rocks. Roughly the size of a small car, Hera is now traveling just 25 to 30 kilometers from the Didymos asteroid system, which consists of a larger asteroid and its smaller companion, Dimorphos.

It has been revealed that the spacecraft has entered its initial observation period, known as the ‘early characterization phase’. During this stage, researchers are collecting essential information about both asteroids, with particular attention to Dimorphos, which NASA deliberately struck with a spacecraft in 2022 to test whether an asteroid’s path could be changed.

“Our aim right now is to gather the major-picture findings of relevance to supporting the mission’s planetary defense goals,” explains mission scientist Michael Kueppers.

“During this phase, our images will reveal for the first time what a small asteroid looks like globally, having experienced a hypervelocity impact in the context of the first asteroid deflection test, when NASA’s DART spacecraft impacted it to change its orbit in 2022.

“Previous predictions by our impact models suggested many different ways the asteroid body might react, but Hera will reveal which forecast was the correct one – if any!”.

Industry observers note that navigating around two small asteroids presents challenges unlike those encountered by spacecraft exploring planets. The biggest difference is gravity, which is extraordinarily weak around these small bodies.

According to recent reports, didymos, the larger asteroid, measures approximately 780 meters across and has gravity roughly 40,000 times weaker than Earth’s. Its smaller moonlet, Dimorphos, is about 151 meters wide, with gravity approximately 200,000 times weaker than Earth’s.

It has been revealed that these conditions make a conventional circular orbit impractical. Instead, Hera moves around the shared center of gravity of the two asteroids at a remarkably slow speed of approximately 12 centimeters per second, comparable to a fast crawling insect.

Rather than continuously curving around its targets, Hera follows a series of nearly straight paths. During a repeating sequence of three days followed by four days, the spacecraft fires its thrusters while moving away from the asteroids, changing direction by 90 degrees. These carefully timed maneuvers produce a series of rectangular flight patterns that keep Hera approximately 25 to 30 kilometers from the asteroid pair.

The technique builds on lessons from ESA’s Rosetta comet mission. Its biggest advantage is safety. If a planned thruster firing fails, Hera will naturally drift farther into space instead of heading toward a potentially damaging collision. The slow flight speed also means that each course correction requires very little fuel.

Hera’s current observations are only the beginning. Next month, the mission is expected to enter its ‘detailed characterization phase’, bringing the spacecraft closer to the asteroids for more thorough measurements.

Industry observers note that during this stage, Hera will begin following more complicated trajectories shaped like bowties. These paths, made up of hyperbolic arcs, will initially take the spacecraft to distances of approximately 20 kilometers from its targets.

The mission is directed from ESA’s ESOC mission control center in Darmstadt, Germany. Controllers communicate with Hera for approximately eight hours each day, despite the spacecraft being about 196.5 million kilometers away.

Those communications travel through four massive Deep Space Antennas, each measuring 35 meters in diameter, at facilities in Argentina, Spain, and Australia.

In a recent development, supporting the controllers is ESA’s Flight Dynamics team. Specialists analyze information transmitted by Hera to pinpoint its location relative to the asteroids. They then calculate the commands needed to guide the spacecraft safely to its next position.

Hera’s primary scientific target is Dimorphos, which became the focus of a groundbreaking planetary defense experiment on September 26, 2022.

That day, NASA’s Double Asteroid Redirection Test (DART) spacecraft collided with Dimorphos. The 580-kilogram spacecraft struck the asteroid at 6.1 kilometers per second, sending a vast cloud of debris spreading across approximately 10,000 kilometers of space.

According to recent reports, the experiment achieved its main objective. The collision shortened Dimorphos’ orbital period around Didymos by approximately 33 minutes, demonstrating that a spacecraft could alter an asteroid’s motion through a direct impact.

However, the results also raised key questions. The change in Dimorphos’ orbit was significantly greater than scientists had predicted, suggesting that the asteroid responded to the collision in ways that existing models did not fully capture.

Researchers still do not know exactly how much physical damage the collision caused. Did DART create a large crater, or did the force of the impact substantially reshape Dimorphos? Scientists also need more precise measurements of the asteroid’s mass, composition, and internal structure to understand why the deflection was so effective.

Answering these questions is essential before the technique, known as ‘kinetic impact’, can become a dependable option for protecting Earth from a potentially hazardous asteroid.

Over the coming months, Hera will conduct a detailed ‘crash site investigation’ of Dimorphos, using its scientific instruments to examine the asteroid and the aftermath of the DART collision.

The spacecraft will also release two shoebox-sized ‘CubeSats’. These miniature spacecraft will approach the asteroids even more closely, gathering additional observations before the mission eventually progresses to landing operations.

Together, the measurements could reveal how Dimorphos absorbed and responded to the impact, helping scientists determine which predictions were accurate and why the asteroid’s orbit changed more than expected.

By turning NASA’s successful experiment into a better-understood planetary defense method, Hera could play an vital role in preparing humanity to deflect an asteroid that might otherwise threaten Earth.

  • Almost all of the major events that changed the trajectory of life on Earth had impossibly tiny beginnings, and the rise of plant life is no exception.
  • Despite the vast evolutionary gulf between them (the two lineages diverged in the middle of the Proterozoic Eon), a newly introduced study published in the journal Nature Communications suggests that the cells derived from red algae and mammals still have the capacity to acquire genetic material through a process known as “horizontal gene transfer.”.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Recent findings suggest that gear-obsessed editors choose every product we review. We may earn commission if you buy from a link. Why Trust Us?

Almost all of the major events that changed the trajectory of life on Earth had impossibly tiny beginnings, and the rise of plant life is no exception. Some 1.5 billion years ago, a eukaryotic cell engulfed a cyanobacterium, which eventually evolved into the chloroplast, the specialized organelle that drives photosynthesis in algae and plants. Other eukaryotic cells, of course, took a very different path, giving rise to all animals and, ultimately, the mammalian cells that make up you and me.

Despite the vast evolutionary gulf between them (the two lineages diverged in the middle of the Proterozoic Eon), a newly introduced study published in the journal Nature Communications suggests that the cells derived from red algae and mammals still have the capacity to acquire genetic material through a process known as “horizontal gene transfer.”.

In a recent development, obviously, most gene transfers in nature move from parents to offspring (fittingly named “vertical gene transfer”), but sometimes cells will acquire traits from other individuals, strains, or even entire species. This is seen most commonly in bacteria that share antibiotic resistance genes, or ARGs, creating troublesome antimicrobial-resistant (or drug-resistant) superbugs in the process. However, other fascinating examples exist, including a parasitic worm that can control its host by swapping genes. In their fresh study, a team of scientists led by researchers at the University of Tokyo explored whether a similar process could take place between cells separated by more than a billion years of evolution, resulting in what the researchers call “planimal” cells.

In a recent development, “We wanted to understand whether entire chromosomes could cross the enormous evolutionary divide between algae and animals and whether animal cells could stably maintain and pass on such foreign genetic material to their daughter cells,” University of Tokyo biologist Sachihiro Matsunaga, senior author of the study, said in a press statement. “These questions are fundamental to understanding how genetic material can move across species boundaries and contribute to evolution.”.

To investigate this possibility, the authors relied on cells derived from the red alga Cyanidioschyzon merolae, along with mammal cells originating from a hamster. Mirroring the primordial event that gave rise to plant life, the researchers allowed the mammalian cell to engulf the alga, after which—surprisingly—cell fusion produced stable hybrid cells. Armed with advanced imaging and genome sequencing, Matsunaga and his team could track how well host mammalian cells retained this algal DNA over subsequent generations. They found that 16.3 million algal base pairs and intact chromosome sequences from all 20 algal chromosomes were retained, and the algal DNA remained detectable through 155 cell generations.

In a recent development, “Plants and animals cannot reproduce with each other, so their chromosomes are never combined through mating. Yet, we have succeeded in creating hybrid chromosomes containing genetic material from both an alga and a mammal,” Matsunaga mentioned. “This demonstrates that even the vast evolutionary divide between plants and animals can be crossed at the level of chromosomes, without reproduction.”.

According to recent reports, the key to the planimal cells’ survival was the epigenetic “gatekeeping” ability of the host cell to essentially silence incorporated foreign DNA. The authors estimate that roughly 96 percent of the algal protein-coding genes were basically offline, but it’s possible that future studies could detect how to flip this gene switch to “on.”.

According to recent reports, “Our ultimate goal is to activate these biological pathways and give animal cells some of the unique abilities of plants and algae,” Matsunaga added. “Imagine animal cells that could sustain photosynthesis for long periods, producing oxygen while using carbon dioxide to make useful organic compounds.”.

Tech Report: An Overlooked Property of Light Could Open the Door to a New Era of Optical Computing

📅 21 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (957 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Scitechdaily

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Monitoring electricity in buried cables could one day become easier thanks to an overlooked magnetic effect in optical fibers, although researchers still need to overcome a major sensitivity challenge.
  • For decades, engineers have used optical fibers to measure magnetic fields around electrical cables, but these sensors generally need to wrap around the conductor to work.
  • The finding, published in Optics Letters, could eventually lead to sensors that sit alongside electrical cables rather than surrounding them.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Monitoring electricity in buried cables could one day become easier thanks to an overlooked magnetic effect in optical fibers, although researchers still need to overcome a major sensitivity challenge.

For decades, engineers have used optical fibers to measure magnetic fields around electrical cables, but these sensors generally need to wrap around the conductor to work. Now, researchers in South Africa have discovered that a magnetic field can also affect light when it points sideways across a fiber, challenging an assumption that has guided optical engineering for more than 50 years.

The finding, published in Optics Letters, could eventually lead to sensors that sit alongside electrical cables rather than surrounding them. It may also offer a latest way to control light for optical computing.

MSc student Mohammed Raiyan Sharif and Professor Mitchell Cox at the University of the Witwatersrand (Wits University) in Johannesburg demonstrated the previously overlooked interaction, known as the transverse Faraday effect. Their research was conducted at the Wits Optical Communication (OC) Lab in the university’s School of Electrical and Information Engineering.

Optical fibers carry internet signals through thin strands of glass, but they can also detect magnetic fields. This sensing ability relies on the Faraday effect, first observed by Michael Faraday in glass in 1845. When a magnetic field points along the direction light travels, it slightly rotates the light’s polarization, or the direction in which its electric field oscillates. Measuring that rotation can reveal the strength of the magnetic field and the electrical current producing it.

Recent findings suggest that A sideways magnetic field was not expected to produce the same effect. To investigate, Sharif and Cox placed strong magnets beside a stationary multimode optical fiber without touching it, then watched the light emerging from the other end.

Industry observers note that multimode fibers have relatively wide glass cores that allow light to travel along many different paths, repeatedly reflecting off the core’s mirror-like boundary. At the output, the overlapping waves create a pattern of bright and dark spots called speckle, similar to the shifting patterns inside a kaleidoscope.

As the researchers rearranged the magnets, a camera recorded changes in that pattern. The sideways magnetic field was somehow altering the light’s behavior inside the fiber.

According to recent reports, “It wasn’t hard to 3D print a rig to test our intuition. Working out the theory for what we were seeing was the challenging part,” states Sharif. “The key was to return to the underlying equations and question assumptions that are usually taken for granted in fiber optics.”.

According to recent reports, the explanation involved a small part of the light wave that a widely used mathematical shortcut ignores. Known as the weak-guidance approximation, this approach assumes that light’s electric field oscillates almost entirely across the fiber, leaving out a tiny component that oscillates along its length.

It has been revealed that the approximation works extremely well when the fiber’s core and surrounding glass have similar refractive indices, which describe how strongly a material slows light. However, Sharif and Cox tested step-index fibers, where the refractive index changes abruptly at the core’s boundary rather than gradually, as it does in graded-index fibers.

According to recent reports, when that difference is large, the normally neglected longitudinal component becomes significant near the core’s edge. By including it in their equations, the researchers highlighted that a sideways magnetic field transfers some of the light’s transverse oscillation into the longitudinal component. This changes how light reflects inside the fiber and, ultimately, the speckle pattern it produces.

The team also distinguished the fresh interaction from the Cotton-Mouton effect, another response to sideways magnetic fields. The Cotton-Mouton effect increases with the square of the magnetic field’s strength, while the transverse Faraday effect increases in direct proportion to it.

Recent findings suggest that their measurements confirmed four predictions. The effect disappeared without a sufficiently strong step in refractive index, became stronger when light entered at steeper angles, occurred for only one polarization relative to the magnetic field, and varied with wavelength in the same way as the conventional Faraday effect.

With a magnetic field of 0.24 tesla, roughly the strength found close to a powerful neodymium magnet, light polarized across the field produced a speckle pattern only about 84% similar to the original.

Industry observers note that “What is surprising is finding an overlooked, useful interaction in such a familiar technology,” says Cox. “It’s quite exciting that there is always something new to learn or discover, and often these things are right under our noses, hidden in the assumptions we have made for decades.”.

One possible application is monitoring electrical currents with fibers laid alongside cables, including those buried in trenches. However, magnetic fields near most cables are much weaker than those used in the experiment, so the sensitivity of a practical sensor remains uncertain.

The researchers also envision replacing permanent magnets with electrical coils, allowing currents to control the patterns of light traveling through a fiber.

“Besides sensing, I think that being able to control different modes (patterns of light) inside the fiber electrically could unlock a new way to do optical computing,” says Cox. “We can model the way light gets distorted when it propagates through fibers, frosted glass windows, or even the atmosphere. If we change our perspective on those models, we can actually use light to do mathematical computations for us, for free.”.

Recent findings suggest that reference: “Transverse Faraday effect in multimode fibers” by Mohammed R. Sharif and Mitchell A. Cox, 30 September 2026, Optics Letters. DOI: 10.1364/OL.611078.

The research was supported by the South African Council for Scientific and Industrial Research (CSIR) and the National Research Foundation (NRF).

In National Geographic’s “Expedition: Saving Our Seas,” it’s all hands on deck

📅 13 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (1066 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Sciencenews

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • This is a human-written story voiced by AI.
  • As documentaries about Earth’s accelerating climate crisis go, Expedition: Saving Our Seas is surprisingly buoyant.
  • The ocean covers more than two-thirds of Earth’s surface.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

This is a human-written story voiced by AI. Got feedback? Take our survey . (See our AI policy here .).

As documentaries about Earth’s accelerating climate crisis go, Expedition: Saving Our Seas is surprisingly buoyant.

The ocean covers more than two-thirds of Earth’s surface. And “as the climate heats up, our seas are under pressure like never before,” narrator Auli’i Cravalho, the voice of the title character in Disney’s Moana, says at the opening of The National Geographic Society’s fresh documentary. The film documents how oceanographers are racing to document and mitigate climate change’s impacts on ocean and coastal habitats.

Expedition: Saving Our Seas premieres November 13 on the National Geographic Channel at 9pm EST and streams the next day on Disney+ and Hulu.

Despite that solemn mission, Expedition: Saving Our Seas is full of hope — and stunning visuals. The documentary offers a window into the scientists’ wonder and joy in their work as they discover new life forms in the depths of the Southern Ocean, or successfully nurture young corals threatened by warming in the Pacific Ocean.

Industry observers note that the film opens with a twist on the usual world map: At the center is one great ocean, surrounded by land. Trivia buffs know Earth has five oceans: the Pacific, Atlantic, Indian, Southern and Arctic. But geographic names aside, these five oceans are just one, linked by a global system of currents known as the Great Ocean Conveyor Belt.

“It’s this giant connected ocean that ignores all of the political boundaries, ignores all of the names we call them,” says Andrew Thurber, a biological oceanographer at the University of California, Santa Barbara, whose research is among those featured in the film.

The documentary loosely follows the current’s path as it zips around the world from project to project.

The first project in the documentary is Thurber’s. He’s on board a research vessel in the frigid Southern Ocean, which rings Antarctica. Using a remotely-operated vehicle dubbed SuBastian, Thurber and his colleagues are scanning the seafloor, hunting for the world’s southernmost hydrothermal vent.

Luján Agusti/National Geographic.

Sources indicate that hydrothermal vents spew superhot, chemically-enriched seawater. In the generally nutrient-poor Southern Ocean, that makes these vents a potential food oasis to support deep sea life.

Throughout the night, as the ROV scans the seafloor, Thurber and his colleagues stay glued to the video it sends back, oohing and aahing as never-before-seen life-forms come into view. “It was a marathon of excitement,” he indicates now.

Then they see it: A large black smoker, the southernmost hydrothermal vent ever found. And all around it: swarms of pregnant female krill.

“That blew all of our minds,” Thurber indicates. Krill are the keystone species of the entire Southern Ocean food web, a crucial food source for baleen whales, seals, penguins and fish. But krill are threatened by both industrial fishing and climate change. This discovery, Thurber says, helps make the case for a marine protected area, a region where fishing and other human activities should be restricted.

In a recent development, from the Southern Ocean, the Great Ocean Conveyor Belt flows thousands of kilometers to the north, where marine ecologist Maiyai Taal Hocheimy is tracking how the rising waters of the Atlantic Ocean are encroaching on Banjul, the capital of The Gambia in West Africa. Her hope is that salt-tolerant mangrove trees along the coast, with their dense network of soil-retaining roots, might help hold back the sea in the coming decades — provided that the community can be enlisted to help maintain the mangroves.

In a recent development, I found Hocheimy’s work especially inspiring because she is working to shape the future of oceanography. In 2017, she founded the GREAT (Gaining Research Experience in Africa for Tomorrow) Institute, the first aquatic and coastal science research institute in The Gambia. The mangrove project recruited young local scientists to help conduct the research.

“The goal is to train the next generation of environmental stewards,” Hocheimy says. “We have to show that mangroves have value, so they’ll understand and want to protect them. It is their future at stake.”.

That sentiment is echoed many times in the film — the importance not only of enlisting young scientists but also centering local scientists who pose new questions that oceanographers who parachute in from other places may not think to ask, claims marine biogeochemist Kristina Brown.

In the documentary, Brown, of the University of Manitoba in Canada, co-leads an expedition to explore the waters of Sherman Basin, a large bay north of the Arctic Circle in Nunavut, Canada. This region has been hunted and fished by Inuit people for centuries.

Sources indicate that but it might change beyond all recognition in the next few decades, Brown claims. So, the local Inuit community invited her to help create the first catalog of what species are present in the waters and on the seafloor. “[It’s] the first project I’ve been involved in where the local community both defined the research questions and have brought their own unique expertise to the research project.”.

Watching how communities around the world are increasingly taking ownership of studies in their own waters was, for me, the most exciting takeaway of this documentary.

“We want to democratize access to the deep sea, to enable people who haven’t had access to these kinds of tools to ask more and upcoming questions,” states Katy Croff Bell, the founder and president of the Ocean Discovery League, a nonprofit ocean exploration group based in Saunderstown, Rhode Island.

It has been revealed that as a result of inaccessibility, little of Earth’s vast ocean has been mapped, particularly the deep sea. Bell’s organization is developing inexpensive technologies such as a hardy little camera and sensor system dubbed DORIS, for Deep Ocean Research and Imaging System. It can descend to 6,000 meters and costs less than $10,000.

Sources indicate that expedition: Saving Our Seas offers just a few scant minutes to each project before moving on around the globe to the next, so there’s no time to learn about each project in depth. But the overall takeaway of watching these vignettes, back to back, is that there is a young, energetic community of scientists taking on the challenge.

Mitigating climate change’s impacts on the oceans is, after all, a race against time. So it’s nice to think we might have all hands on deck.

💡 Key Takeaways

  • Sources indicate that high cholesterol can silently damage blood vessels for decades, increasing the risk of heart attacks and strokes without causing noticeable symptoms.
  • It has been revealed that A newly approved once-daily pill could provide another option.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

A pill taken before breakfast cut “bad” cholesterol by nearly two-thirds in a trial of people already taking statins.

Sources indicate that high cholesterol can silently damage blood vessels for decades, increasing the risk of heart attacks and strokes without causing noticeable symptoms. Much of that danger comes from excess LDL (“bad”) cholesterol, which contributes to fatty plaque buildup inside artery walls. Although statins help millions of people control their cholesterol, some patients need additional treatment to bring their levels down.

It has been revealed that A newly approved once-daily pill could provide another option. Lipfendra (enlicitide) reduced LDL cholesterol by nearly 65% in a clinical trial involving adults already taking statins. Approved by the FDA on July 16, 2026, it is the first oral medication in a powerful class of cholesterol treatments previously available only through injections.

Enlicitide targets PCSK9, a protein that influences how efficiently the liver removes LDL cholesterol from the bloodstream. Normally, PCSK9 promotes the destruction of LDL receptors on liver cells. When these receptors are lost, the liver becomes less effective at clearing circulating cholesterol.

By blocking PCSK9, enlicitide allows more LDL receptors to remain active, helping the liver remove additional cholesterol from the blood. Unlike earlier PCSK9 inhibitors that require injections, enlicitide uses a specialized macrocyclic peptide formulation with absorption-enhancing ingredients, allowing the medication to be taken orally.

It has been revealed that A review published in Annals of Pharmacotherapy found that enlicitide reduced LDL cholesterol by 57.1% to 64.6% after 24 weeks across clinical trials. These reductions were comparable to those achieved with injectable PCSK9 inhibitors.

Industry observers note that in a direct comparison involving patients already taking statins, LDL cholesterol fell by approximately 65% with enlicitide. By comparison, reductions were about 28% with ezetimibe and 6% with bempedoic acid, two other oral medications used to manage high cholesterol.

In a recent development, the review examined research identified through PubMed, Embase, Web of Science, and Cochrane through July 17, 2026. Participants included adults with elevated cholesterol and those with heterozygous familial hypercholesterolemia, an inherited condition that causes unusually high LDL cholesterol levels from birth and increases the risk of premature cardiovascular disease.

In the largest trial, adverse effects occurred at similar rates among participants receiving enlicitide and those taking a placebo. However, a separate study involving people with inherited high cholesterol reported more diarrhea and dizziness among those receiving the medication. Longer-term monitoring will help establish its safety with continued use.

It has been revealed that enlicitide must be taken in the morning on an empty stomach. Patients may drink water, black coffee, or plain tea with the medication but must wait at least 30 minutes before consuming food or other beverages. A 30-day supply carries a list price of $315, although actual costs depend on insurance coverage.

In a recent development, while clinical trials have established that enlicitide substantially reduces LDL cholesterol, researchers have not yet determined whether it also prevents heart attacks and strokes. An ongoing cardiovascular outcomes trial is investigating whether its cholesterol-lowering effects translate into fewer serious cardiovascular events.

Reference: “Enlicitide: The First Oral PCSK9i for Lowering Low-Density Lipoprotein Cholesterol” by Rachel C. Lucas, Mia E. Lussier, Azadeh Nasuhidehnavi and Taylor M. Clark, 14 October 2026, Annals of Pharmacotherapy. DOI: 10.1177/10600280261494015.
