American science is broken. Meet the people fixing it

📅 19 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 17 min read (3444 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Sciencenews

⏱️ ~17 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • In a recent development, this is a human-written story voiced by AI.
  • Industry observers note that the February sun was setting outside her family’s West Virginia home when Rebecca Lindsey found out she was being fired in 75 minutes.
  • According to recent reports, “Every week, it was like, ‘This is the week we’re all going to get fired,’ ” says Lindsey, who had worked as a contractor and later a civil servant at the National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration for nearly 15 years.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In a recent development, this is a human-written story voiced by AI. Got feedback? Take our survey . (See our AI policy here .).

Industry observers note that the February sun was setting outside her family’s West Virginia home when Rebecca Lindsey found out she was being fired in 75 minutes. Lindsey, who until early 2025 managed the federal government’s climate.gov website, had just begun to think her job might be safe during the second Trump administration.

According to recent reports, “Every week, it was like, ‘This is the week we’re all going to get fired,’ ” says Lindsey, who had worked as a contractor and later a civil servant at the National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration for nearly 15 years. “Every time you would hear the rumor and then it wouldn’t happen, you would think … maybe this is all just talk.”.

According to recent reports, but at 3:45 p.m. on February 27, 2025, Lindsey and around 800 of her NOAA colleagues received a mass termination email saying they no longer “fit the Agency’s current needs.” In June, Lindsey’s sister and the data visualization lead for the project, Mary Lindsey, was fired alongside the remaining climate.gov contractors. The website URL was redirected, hiding the site — and its decades’ worth of climate visualizations, educational tools and extreme weather trackers — from the public.

The Lindsey sisters decided to fight back. Along with another terminated NOAA employee, they split a $65,000 grant from the nonprofit Surge Climate Talent and debuted a crowdfunding campaign to rebuild and patch climate.gov. The site, now called climate.us, notched one million views in its first month.

According to recent reports, but as proud as they are of their work, the project is a patch, not a fix. Rebecca Lindsey predicts it would take at least seven employees and $1.8 million annually to resume 80 percent of the old site’s work. “Climate.gov was more than just a website; it was a climate literacy program,” she says. To rescue the full mission, they still have a long way to go.

Industry observers note that courtesy of M. Lindsey and R. Lindsey.

According to recent reports, the Lindsey sisters are far from the only tale of makeshift resilience. Over the last year, untold numbers of U.S. scientists and their supporters have rebuilt data dashboards, formed recommendation groups for childhood vaccines and screenings, and doled out research funds for hundreds of stranded early-career scientists. They’ve reconstituted committees to advise space missions, rehomed key reports on climate and Arctic science, and even turned to social media to spread public health alerts in the wake of a massive realignment of the federal science enterprise.

“I don’t think anyone could have foreseen the amount of destruction and deliberate breaking down of norms and infrastructure” over the last two years, says Christina Madison, a clinical pharmacist and public health communicator known on social media as The Public Health Pharmacist.

In a recent development, since January 2025, the second Trump administration has frozen or rescinded billions of dollars in research funding on topics from climate change to vaccine hesitancy and is trying to redirect it — often without congressional approval — to administration priorities such as artificial intelligence and quantum computing. During deliberations for the FY2026 and FY2027 budgets, the White House proposed slashing future science funding by one-third.

“When this was first starting, it really, truly felt like an alternate universe,” says Sean O’Leary, a pediatric infectious disease researcher at the University of Colorado Anschutz. “The science was always what drove the decision making, and now we’re at a place where it’s not.”.

Recent findings suggest that in 2025 alone, the federal government shed some 20 percentof its science workforce. And in May 2026, the Office of Management and Budget proposed a sweeping set of rules to expand the authority of federal political appointees in selecting science grants.

Approximate proportion of the scientific workforce who left federal service in 2025.

Yet some researchers see the destruction as an opportunity to rebuild their corners of U.S. science — or even reimagine it, states Michael Osterholm, an epidemiologist at the University of Minnesota in Minneapolis. “If there’s any good that can come out of what has been a horrible situation, it’s that it’s given us time and provided a pause to think through clearly: Is this the way we want to continue?”.

University of Ottawa ecologist Julien Martin spent a decade building a respected lab that probed how social behaviors affect the evolution of bushy-tailed, cat-sized rodents called marmots. So when the National Science Foundation began its sweeping grant cuts, Martin found himself doing something unexpected: uploading cute marmot videos to OnlyFans, an online video subscription platform better known for hosting pornography.

In a recent development, the effort, called OnlyMarms, netted $6,000 — a mere drop in the funding bucket. But the project went viral, leading outside supporters to launch a cryptocurrency token that earned the lab an additional $150,000. And direct donations, including an anonymous $300,000 gift, gave the lab enough to fund one Ph.D. student’s entire degree.

“When you see that so much money could be obtained by doing essentially nothing about science, it’s quite shocking,” Martin notes. He welcomes the support, but having to spend so much time on non-research tasks has also felt demeaning. “Sometimes, you have to question: Is the science funding broken? Are we just competing for pennies?”.

Recent findings suggest that in 2025, the National Institutes of Health and the NSF canceled or suspended more than 7,800 existing grants, totaling billions of dollars. (Some 5,200 grants were later reinstated.) Each agency issued roughly a quarter fewer grants in 2025 than their previous 10-year averages.

Industry observers note that universities and research centers were hit hard. “It was really dire,” indicates Emily Young, who leads medical research grantmaking at the San Diego-based Prebys Foundation. In phone calls with researchers, many told her they had halted ongoing experiments, such as developing measles vaccines for people with autoimmune disorders.

But the thing that really stood out, Young notes, was how the sudden drop in funding was affecting postdocs and early-career researchers. “Young people were going from feeling like they had an avenue for a really promising career … to feeling like they were in a worthless career.”.

It has been revealed that so, in May 2025, the foundation awarded $7 million total in emergency grants to seven local institutions, including San Diego State University, the University of California, San Diego and Scripps Research. The grants targeted more than 80 research programs involving early- and mid-career scientists that were facing hundreds of millions of dollars in lost federal funding.

Industry observers note that larger science philanthropies also stepped into the breach. The Gordon and Betty Moore Foundation gave $55 million total to 30 universities to support 400 postdoctoral researchers. The Alfred P. Sloan and Spencer foundations, among others, partnered to provide 83 quick-turnaround grants of around $25,000 each to researchers whose NSF education grants had been canceled.

Some wealthy universities also offered bridge funding to their researchers; Johns Hopkins University gave awards up to $250,000 to individuals with unexpected funding gaps, and the Yale School of Medicine arranged to fund up to 90 percent of terminated or frozen NIH grants.

In a recent development, after the first bout of funding chaos, science philanthropy Schmidt Sciences declared a more ambitious approach: to develop the science themselves. In January 2026, they revealed intends to construct three ground-based observatories and a space telescope larger than NASA’s Hubble by the end of the decade. The space telescope alone will cost hundreds of millions of dollars and provide open-access data to scientists worldwide, with a special focus on exoplanets and transient events like supernovas.

In November 2026, the philanthropy opened its first round of funding for early-career scientists using the observatory system; individual awards will total up to $2.5 million each.

“Originally, the hope was we would play a more classic philanthropic role,” says Arpita Roy, an astronomer who directs the Astrophysics & Space Center at Schmidt Sciences. But given the federal funding landscape, she says, “it became pretty clear to us, if we really think these things need to exist in the world … then we need to build them out.”.

In a recent development, while private funding can be a lifeline, Young notes, it’s still a temporary measure at best. “We are not going to fill the vacuum of federal funding,” she says. “There is simply not enough philanthropic resource out there to do that.”.

According to recent reports, in 1995, the American Academy of Pediatrics and the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention made a consequential decision: Rather than publish independent recommendations for childhood vaccines, as they had since the 1960s, they would problem one set jointly. Over the next 30 years, a group called the Advisory Committee on Immunization Practices advised the CDC, with academy input, to expand its recommendations to include chickenpox, hepatitis A and pneumococcal infections. Cases of the three dropped by more than 90 percent, saving thousands of lives.

But in June 2025, Secretary of Health and Human Services Robert F. Kennedy Jr., an outspoken vaccine critic, fired all 17 members of ACIP and replaced many with vaccine skeptics. Kennedy also dismissed the academy representatives that informed the group.

Recent findings suggest that “Essentially, we had no voice anymore,” recalls O’Leary, the pediatric infectious disease researcher at the University of Colorado Anschutz. He also serves as the AAP’s immunization schedule editor. “So we made a decision to not participate until we could say, ‘OK, this is a body that can be trusted.’ ”.

In July 2025, the academy and other public health groups sued over the ACIP firings. The committee was unable to meet due to the lawsuit, and over the next six months, the CDC removed recommendations from its childhood vaccination schedule including hepatitis A and B, COVID-19 and meningococcal disease. The American Academy of Pediatrics issued its own schedule including those vaccines in January 2026.

Svetlana Repnitskaya/Getty Images Plus.

Recent findings suggest that the loss of trustworthy federal recommendations leaves “an impossible gap to fill,” O’Leary says. But when it came to stepping in, “from my perspective, there was not an alternative.” The academy has since collaborated with the Vaccine Integrity Project, a new group led by Osterholm, to conduct the scientific reviews that inform vaccine recommendations.

Vaccines weren’t the only childhood health matter to get a shakeup. In April 2025, HHS terminated the Advisory Committee on Heritable Disorders in Newborns and Children, which formulates newborn screening recommendations for genetic disorders, many of which can be deadly or disabling. Currently, some 98 percent of U.S.-born infants are screened at birth.

When the genetics community raised concerns, Cynthia Powell, a retired pediatric geneticist at the University of North Carolina School of Medicine in Chapel Hill, gathered around 15 representatives of professional medical societies to create the Newborn Screening Collaborative. With support from the American College of Medical Genetics and Genomics, the group began meeting in early 2026.

It has been revealed that while the collaborative cannot give direct recommendations to HHS, it hopes to conduct evidence reviews for states and the small, parent-led advocacy groups that form around rare diseases, Powell states. It plans to focus on conditions that already have treatments under development, like a rare metabolic disorder known as Sanfilippo syndrome type A.

Industry observers note that approximate number of NIH and NSF grants canceled or suspended in 2025. Some 5,200 have since been reinstated.

“This Newborn Screening Collaborative is another effort not to leave a complete void,” says Jewel Mullen, an epidemiologist at the University of Texas at Austin who was lead editor on a May 2025 newborn screening report for the National Academies of Sciences, Engineering and Medicine.

Industry observers note that other researchers are filling gaps in awareness about public health threats. A philanthropy-backed group called the Evidence Collective posted about the diarrhea-causing cyclosporiasis outbreak before the CDC’s Health Alert Network did. The collective, made up of more than 30 medical communicators, has more than 10 million followers across social media and notched 11 billion impressions in 2025.

Industry observers note that “I don’t think that we will ever be able to fully replace the infrastructure that was there through the federal government,” says Madison, a founding member of the collective. But “there is a concerted effort now to look at: How do we take the momentum that we have with these organizations, and then make it sustainable?”.

Sources indicate that although stopgap measures are succeeding so far, scientists see them as Band-Aids at best. “We’re going to do it for as long as we’re needed,” Osterholm says. But “I look forward to the day when we’re not going to be needed anymore.”.

In a recent development, in April 2025, nearly 400 scientists working on the National Climate Assessment, a recurring, congressionally mandated report, received an email that it was being reevaluated and they were being released from their work. One of them — Rutgers University climate scientist Bob Kopp — wasn’t surprised. “I don’t think you have to speculate very far” to know why, Kopp says. He cites a directive in the White House’s 2027 budget request to “stop wasting biological and environmental research resources on climate change.”.

However, “there was an immediate and deep sentiment by the science community to continue the work,” notes environmental engineer Costa Samaras of Carnegie Mellon University in Pittsburgh, who had also been involved with the climate report. He and colleagues asked the American Geophysical Union and the American Meteorological Society to help organize the U.S. Climate Collection, a new set of papers from scientists about climate research, risks and solutions that will keep the public informed until federal assessments resume.

While the work is promising, “a volunteer effort of 170 scientists cannot substitute for a $30 million effort of 600 people,” Kopp says.

The American Geophysical Union similarly stepped in with crucial financing for the Arctic Report Card, an annual report from NOAA that has provided information about the changing Arctic since 2006. Its editors were blindsided when they found out during a routine meeting in August 2026 that NOAA was withdrawing its support.

AGU’s in-kind offer to support the project just one month later was “tremendous,” notes Twila Moon, a glaciologist at the National Snow and Ice Data Center in Boulder, Colo., who edits the report card. “But [it] is not a kind of model that is sustainable into the future.”.

AGU President Brandon Jones agrees. Nevertheless, at the time, the organization “had this sense of what was moral, what was right, what was ethical,” Jones claims. And given AGU’s resources, “it seemed like it was our turn to show up and step up and act like the union that we’ve always been.”.

The Planetary Society, a nonprofit space advocacy organization based in Pasadena, Calif., took the lead on several committees that NASA dropped. In January, the agency cited executive orders as it withdrew financial and logistical support from eight groups of space scientists and experts that advised NASA’s planning teams on exploring asteroids, comets and planets.

“It was pretty well-managed and organized [before], and then really fell apart because of the intrusion of the executive orders,” states Jack Kiraly, chief of advocacy at the Planetary Society. The organization now hosts the advisory groups’ websites, documents and meetings. “We’ve basically been having to reinvent this whole system.”.

Chris Gunn, Courtesy of Schmidt Sciences.

Climate.us isn’t the only site saving federal data. In November 2024, many environmental organizations “started preparing for the worst,” states Brittany Janis, executive director of the Open Environmental Data Project. Her group and nine others banded together to create the Public Environmental Data Partners, a network of 400 volunteers that archive environmental data and tools they suspected “would probably be on the chopping block.”.

It has been revealed that in February 2025, the Environmental Protection Agency deleted a tool called EJScreen, which maps places where people face high levels of risk from environmental burdens such as hazardous waste and ozone. Within 48 hours, the partnership had stood up EJScreen on a new website, using open-source files to reverse engineer and refine the data pipelines. It has since received 1,000 views a month, Janis notes.

In a recent development, nearly $2 million in philanthropic funding has helped the project pay staff, host data and hire engineers. It has restored the Federal Emergency Management Agency’s Future Risk Index, which projects county-level economic losses from climate change; the White House Council on Environmental Quality’s Climate and Economic Justice Screening Tool, which identifies communities overburdened by pollution; and the Department of Homeland Security’s Homeland Infrastructure Foundation-Level Data tool, which maps infrastructure at risk of natural disasters.

In a recent development, “We should not misunderstand the administration’s closing off of this data [to mean] that they don’t think data is important,” Janis indicates. “They recognize how important it is — and how valuable it is to causes that they disagree with.”.

At the University of Chicago, the Data Mirror Project preserves datasets larger than one terabyte, including those from the U.S. Census Bureau and the National Park Service. The project has a guiding principle: LOCKSS, which stands for lots of copies keeps stuff safe, states colead Lisa Chinn, who is head of research data services at the university library. An agency doesn’t have to delete its data to create problems, she adds. Firing website staff can lead to wonky links, corrupted files and pages that degrade into Wingdings gibberish.

The thought of losing all that data can be stressful, Janis says, but “there’s a lot of parachutes that have gone out.”.

Even as researchers, volunteers and scientific organizations pick up the pieces of the federal science enterprise, some are already imagining new ways of shaping it. “The world was not perfect in 2024,” says Rutgers’ Kopp. “Reconstruction is an opportunity to improve upon the way things are done.”.

According to recent reports, to Mullen, the epidemiologist at the University of Texas at Austin, transparency is key. New bodies like the Vaccine Integrity Project and the Newborn Screening Collaborative should make their meetings and deliberations as open as possible, she notes, especially when “people think that those with the loudest voices or the biggest wallets are going to be the ones that have the greatest influence behind the scenes.”.

Powell, of the Newborn Screening Collaborative, is hoping for greater efficiency in the disease recommendation process. Previously, it could take as long as three years to bring a condition from an initial vote to a final recommendation; with the collaborative, she hopes it could take one to three months.

Janis, of the Open Environmental Data Project, hopes to develop more creative and flexible data tools for researchers based on their needs. And Madison from the Evidence Collective and Martin of OnlyMarms believe that the science infrastructure needs to diversify its funding sources to prevent future shocks.

“If we really think these things need to exist in the world … then we need to build them out.”.

However, Janis notes that there are inherent risks in having the private sector support public goods such as open information. And Kopp warns that “attempts to replace something that was well-functioning … are not going to necessarily end up with something that is better or even as good as what was there before.”.

At the end of the day, one of the key elements in establishing a upcoming science system is “faith that you will still exist in a year or 10 years or maybe even 20 years,” claims Katharine Jacobs, an environmental scientist who directed a previous National Climate Assessment under President Obama. Without stable institutional funding, “we are all essentially wasting our time, bashing our heads against the wall, trying to create a system that we can’t support,” Jacobs says.

For the Lindsey sisters, being involved in public service — even outside the government aegis — has been empowering, especially during what they see as an otherwise dark period for science.

They have raised more than $600,000 from individual donations since August 2025. And in February, they received a one-time grant from the Doris Duke Foundation and others that will cover their salaries and benefits until February 2027.

Industry observers note that “If we can get the money, I can see us doing this indefinitely,” Rebecca Lindsey states. She still hopes to retire one day, and she fights off worries that the government might come knocking about their unsanctioned work. But “we had a public that trusted us,” she says about jumping into the fray. “It was a risk worth taking.”.

What satellites leave behind

📅 19 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 16 min read (3251 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Astronomy

⏱️ ~16 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • It was the lithium that gave it away, claims Daniel Murphy, an atmospheric chemist at the National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration.
  • It was early 2023, in Fairbanks, Alaska, in the deep blue of winter, and Murphy and his colleagues had just sent a plane through the stratosphere, the atmospheric stratum 6 to 31 miles (10 to 50 kilometers) above Earth’s surface where the protective ozone layer lies.
  • Their experiment came as interest was growing in controversial proposals to cool the planet by injecting certain aerosols into the atmosphere — a form of geoengineering.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It was the lithium that gave it away, claims Daniel Murphy, an atmospheric chemist at the National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration.

It was early 2023, in Fairbanks, Alaska, in the deep blue of winter, and Murphy and his colleagues had just sent a plane through the stratosphere, the atmospheric stratum 6 to 31 miles (10 to 50 kilometers) above Earth’s surface where the protective ozone layer lies.

Their experiment came as interest was growing in controversial proposals to cool the planet by injecting certain aerosols into the atmosphere — a form of geoengineering. The team hoped to get a baseline measurement of the chemistry of the upper atmosphere, before any geoengineering experiments altered the hard-to-reach atmospheric layer.

The lithium highlighted they were too late.

Sources indicate that the team expected to find trace amounts of metals naturally deposited by meteoroids, which constantly bombard and burn up in Earth’s atmosphere. But their data revealed way more lithium in stratospheric particles than is typically present in meteoroids.

In a recent development, “That’s what led us to the other metals,” Murphy claims. Analyzing their samples, they also found higher than expected levels of aluminum, plus significant amounts of other metals like copper and lead that are scarcely found in meteoroids and must have come from some other source. Then there were the more exotic metals like niobium and hafnium, which appeared in their samples in the same ratio as in an alloy used to manufacture rocket engine nozzles.

The data pointed to an obvious culprit: human-made objects such as satellites and spent rocket stages that fall back to Earth from orbit and reenter the atmosphere. On the way down, they wear away and disintegrate under the heat of friction — a process known as ablation.

Later that year in the Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences (PNAS), Murphy and his colleagues reported that 10% of stratospheric aerosol particles carried metals from spacecraft.

The number was shocking, but not altogether surprising. Reentries have been rising sharply in recent years as corporations and countries began launching megaconstellations of thousands of satellites, like SpaceX’s Starlink. And all those satellites will inevitably deorbit.

Since Murphy and his colleagues’ 2023 report, it’s become clear that human-made satellites are now dumping more of certain metals into the upper atmosphere than meteoroids naturally do. This influx has raised concerns that the metals might catalyze chemical reactions that destroy ozone, alter cloud formation, or boost or buffer the greenhouse effect.

In a recent development, researchers say it’s too soon to know for sure if the metals are a serious environmental problem. But megaconstellations are growing faster than our ability to close these knowledge gaps.

At the same time, the uncertainty over whether regulators might have to act presents a big risk to the space industry, says Martin Ross of the Aerospace Corporation, a research and development nonprofit based in El Segundo, California, and a co-author of the 2023 study. “We would call it an enterprise risk,” says Ross, “in that the longer we wait to see if there is something going on, the bigger the mitigation will be — if there needs to be any mitigation — down the line.”.

From our vantage point on Earth, space may be incomprehensibly vast, but the orbital environment is not.

According to recent reports, six years ago, according to the U.S. Space Force’s public catalog, there were some 13,700 trackable objects circling in low Earth orbit; last year, the number had climbed to nearly 25,000. Disposing of satellites in the atmosphere reduces overcrowding and the risk of uncontrolled objects crashing into each other — and potentially setting off a chain of collisions that wipe out key space-based technologies or turn Earth orbit into an impenetrable debris field.

RELATED: Our increasingly cluttered skies.

“Reentry is the only sustainable, short-term way of cleaning up the orbital environment,” states José Pedro Ferreira, a doctoral candidate in astronautical engineering at the University of Southern California (USC) in Los Angeles, who left an industry job for academia in the early 2020s when it became clear that reentry could have unintended consequences. “We need to do it, otherwise we may undermine our capability of accessing orbit.”.

But operators are also typically held responsible by their national regulators for any damages their spacecraft cause on the ground, and for decades the industry has designed spacecraft to burn up as much as possible in the atmosphere to minimize the risk to lives and infrastructure on the ground, a principle known as design for demise.

As a result, the space industry has long perceived its impacts to Earth as minimal. But in the age of megaconstellations, that’s no longer the case.

“As with everything, we live in a closed system,” says Ferreira, “and things do not disappear.”.

In a recent development, spaceX debuted its first 60 satellites into orbit in May 2019 to bring internet to even remote regions of the globe; less than a decade later, Starlink’s constellation is more than 10,000 satellites strong. Starlink already comprises roughly two-thirds of active satellites, and SpaceX plans to grow it to as many as 42,000. Other countries and corporations are not far behind: Amazon Leo is authorized by the Federal Communications Commission (FCC) to operate roughly 7,700 satellites; China has plans to deploy some 28,000.

Not only are we launching more than ever, but we’re also bringing spacecraft back down faster than ever before.

Recent findings suggest that for decades, spacecraft have been designed to burn up as much as possible upon reentry to minimize risks to those on the ground. As a result, the space industry has long perceived its impacts to Earth as minimal. But in the age of megaconstellations, that’s no longer the case.

In a recent development, historically, satellite operators had what Ferreira calls a “gentleman’s agreement” to deorbit their spacecraft within 25 years of mission termination to prevent orbital clutter. Recently, some national authorities have begun enforcing even tighter timelines. The FCC, for example, now enforces a five-year window.

“If you have 50,000 satellites in orbit, which is almost surely going to be reached in the not too distant future, with a design lifetime of five years,” Murphy indicates, “that would mean a satellite would be reentering and burning up in the atmosphere on average more than once an hour.”.

Sources indicate that operators of megaconstellations may use even shorter timelines for deorbiting satellites, according to Ferreira, bringing them down at the first sign of malfunction. “Which is great from a standpoint of orbital sustainability,” he claims, “but it starts raising the question more and more about what the impacts are in the atmosphere.”.

There are reasons to be concerned.

In a recent development, aluminum, for example, which makes up the bulk of most spacecraft, may form aluminum oxides as it breaks down during ablation, which can kick-start a chain of chemical reactions that eat away at ozone, Earth’s main shield against UV radiation. Some atmospheric models suggest that metals from spacecraft in stratospheric particles could seed polar stratospheric clouds, further accelerating ozone depletion.

In a recent development, injecting aluminum into the upper atmosphere is also the basis of many controversial geoengineering aims. Aluminum compounds would block radiation from the Sun, which could cool down our warming planet. But they might also entrap radiation reflected off the surface of the ocean, which could increase surface temperatures. Opposition to geoengineering has so far stymied any field experiments, but with the number of reentries rising from a few hundred to many thousands per year, an uncontrolled geoengineering experiment on a grand scale may have already begun.

According to recent reports, “The metals are at the same altitude range as the ozone layer, so we have to be concerned about what they would do,” Murphy says. “We don’t know it’s bad, but we don’t know it isn’t bad either.”.

Sources indicate that one reason it’s so difficult to predict the impacts of ablation is that we don’t yet understand what happens to spacecraft during ablation. “We reenter things all the time and we have been since the moment we started launching spacecraft,” notes Stijn Lemmens, a space debris mitigation analyst at the European Space Agency (ESA). “It’s fascinating, for something which is so ubiquitous, how little we actually know about it, and how little we used to care about it.”.

Operators have long been incentivized to design spacecraft to burn up as much as possible in the atmosphere, and decades of this design for demise ethos has given the space industry a solid idea of how much material — or how little — will make it to the ground when objects burn through the atmosphere.

Sources indicate that but in terms of that material that is ablated, “we’re really in the dark,” says Ross. Previous studies have suggested that around 90% of the bodies of orbiting satellites and spent upper stages could be vaporized, later condensing into the nanosized particles the team detected. But, says Ross, “we really don’t understand how these vehicles melt, how they break apart, how they form smoke trails.”.

In a recent development, to quantify the impacts on the atmosphere, researchers start with atmospheric models and then add ablated material, examining how those particles interact with the natural stratospheric background via complex chemical reactions and physical processes like mixing. But the outputs of the atmospheric models are presently held back by our limited understanding of the fiery, complex process of ablation — details like what compounds are being emitted and what size particles are being formed. “We’re basically guessing at this point,” Ross says. “And we’re getting to the limit of what we can do with guessing.”.

In a recent development, to do better, scientists are developing latest models of the physics and chemistry of ablation itself. At USC, Ferreira and his colleagues model how ablation produces aluminum oxides in the upper atmosphere, providing atmospheric researchers with inputs for both emissions and particle size. In a 2024 study in Geophysical Research Letters, the team reported that a 550-pound (250 kilograms) satellite — about the size of your average megaconstellation satellite — could deposit some 66 pounds (30 kg) of aluminum oxide nanoparticles in the upper atmosphere. Such particles could remain aloft for upwards of 30 years, potentially catalyzing ozone-destroying reactions as they settle throughout the stratosphere for decades after reentry.

Recent findings suggest that but state-of-the-art ablation models don’t always agree on what products are being formed, according to Ross. A model from researchers at the University of Leeds in the U.K. suggests that aluminum hydroxide, rather than aluminum oxide, may be the main byproduct.

Industry observers note that to validate ablation models and get more useful data from atmospheric models, we need more measurements from reentries. How an object breaks apart as it tumbles through the air is a messy process — a product of astrophysics, fluid mechanics, materials science, and engineering. “You cannot reproduce it on Earth,” Lemmens says. “There is no facility large enough to, in one assessment, combine all the effects.”.

That means scientists need to measure ablation where it’s actually taking place — “take instruments and put them on airplanes and go out and watch these things reenter,” Ross notes.

Sources indicate that since the beginning of the Space Age, these kinds of measurements have only been taken a handful of times. Observing space objects from an airplane as they streak through the atmosphere is difficult work — and potentially dangerous. Most reentering objects are uncontrolled, making it hard to predict exactly where the object will hit the atmosphere and how much of it will burn up in the process. Researchers need a degree of certainty to avoid sending a plane full of scientists and sensors up into a debris field. “These types of reentries, which are destructive and still predictable so that you can get close, are extremely rare,” Lemmens states.

Sources indicate that but in 2024, ESA got lucky. The first of four Cluster II satellites — debuted in 2000 to study Earth’s magnetosphere — was poised to reenter the atmosphere, and the agency had a pretty good idea of exactly where and when it would break up over the southern Pacific Ocean.

It has been revealed that “We could get close,” Lemmens states. “The drawback is it was in broad daylight, which had not been attempted before on this level of detail.”.

In daytime, the team would have no visual confirmation of reentry, and it would be harder to get clean data than at night. The team had to trust they were pointing their instruments at the right spot, and then look at their data after the fact to see if they caught it. “In the end, it’s a leap of faith,” Lemmens indicates. “You predict as well as you can, you fly the plane as well as you can, but in the end, you do it all in the blind,” he says.

On Sept. 8, a team of scientists took off from Easter Island on a modified Dassault Falcon 900 business jet packed with instruments, and pointed their cameras just above the bright blue horizon roughly 500 miles (800 km) away.

The team used spectroscopic instruments to identify which vapors were coming from the ablating satellite. Since the team knew the material makeup of the satellite, they could gauge its surface temperatures during reentry, as the appearance of specific ions would indicate a certain material had reached its melting point.

According to recent reports, altogether, they captured about 20 seconds of the reentry. Two more satellites from the same cluster were set to reenter within 24 hours of each other on Aug. 31 and Sept. 1, 2026, giving ESA another opportunity to capture more of the reentry process and to fully reconstruct the breakup.

For researchers, one upside to the rapid and unmitigated increase in satellite reentries is more opportunities to capture the process in action.

Recent findings suggest that some of the best data yet to come will be collected by ESA’s Draco mission, in which the agency aims to build and launch a satellite with the “sole purpose of falling apart again,” says Lemmens. Draco will launch in 2027 with an indestructible capsule that will survive reentry, protecting the data collected from the surface of the satellite as it’s torn apart by the atmosphere.

Sources indicate that researchers will be able to combine these onboard data with remote observations, using them to improve or validate existing models of ablation. “That means we, for the first time, will actually have the full story without any ambiguities,” Lemmens states.

Once a scientific consensus is reached, then mitigation measures, whether technological or regulatory, can be deployed.

In a recent development, if research confirms that one material or another in spacecraft is particularly damaging to the atmosphere, for example, space operators can remove and replace it. “That was the basis of the success of the Montreal Protocol,” notes Ross.

Industry observers note that after scientists discovered a hole in the ozone layer in the 1980s, every country in the world signed on to the Montreal Protocol, an international agreement to control the ozone-depleting substances humans were emitting into the atmosphere. The hole has been shrinking ever since. Signed in 1987, the agreement is widely considered one of the most successful environmental treaties to date. Since then, however, other global climate agreements have not fared as well.

According to recent reports, still, many remain optimistic, including Ross. He points to the commercial space industry’s track record of working with regulators and astronomers to reduce space debris and light pollution. “There is some current flowing in those lines,” he claims.

RELATED: Can robots save Earth orbit?

In a recent development, some operators have already expressed a commitment to acting on whatever guidelines come out of research on the atmospheric risks. “The difficulty that I have as a responsible operator is, in this particular case, I don’t know what to do,” Vijay Thakur, a technical authority at French satellite corporation Eutelsat, said at an October 2025 panel at the Secure World Foundation’s 7th Summit for Space Sustainability in Paris. There are clear brightness limits he can follow to mitigate impacts to the astronomical community, he noted, but no such guidelines exist yet for atmospheric impacts.

“I want to put the right technical requirements, for me as the operator customer, onto industry so they can build what I need to operate and take it up and bring it back down without damaging anything from 0 kilometers to the von Kármán line,” Thakur stated, referring to the commonly accepted boundary of outer space at 62 miles high (100 km). “Help.”.

There are some design tweaks currently available that could reduce emissions and help more of each spacecraft survive reentry, including non-ablative heat shields and inflatable aerodynamic decelerators, according to Adam Mitchell, a materials and processes evaluation engineer at ESA.

Of course, the more of a spacecraft that survives reentry, the greater the risk on the ground during uncontrolled reentries — and most reentries are uncontrolled. “There is this balance between sustainability and safety, but when it comes to human safety, there is no compromise at all,” Chris Young, space sustainability senior lead at the U.K. Space Agency, noted at the same Secure World Foundation panel. “Design for demise has to take priority.”.

Satellite builders could also consider replacing problematic metals — but that comes with its own trade-offs. In 2024, the world’s first wooden satellite, LignoSat, launched to orbit in a partnership between Kyoto University and Japanese logging firm Sumitomo Forestry. A cube of magnolia wood panels, LignoSat will give researchers insights into how well wood holds up in the space environment, and how cleanly it burns up in the atmosphere. Carbon fiber is another material of interest, according to Ferreira. But these organic materials may release black carbon into the upper atmosphere, which may absorb sunlight or reflect it, depending on the structure the carbon takes.

It has been revealed that ross thinks we can close the remaining knowledge gaps in short order — and that those lessons can be applied almost immediately. “We can do that before the next generation of satellites comes along,” he says, “but we just need the resources.”.

A cultural revolution is coming for the industry, regardless of what’s discovered about the impacts to the atmosphere. “The one-use, nonrecyclable culture that we have in space, of, ‘We’ll launch something to space with rare Earth minerals that are of limited supply and then burn them all up in the atmosphere after one use,’ that is unsustainable,” said Young.

A sustainable future — one that balances both Earth and space sustainability — will involve creating something we haven’t quite nailed yet in our earthbound industries. “We need to move beyond the single-use mindset that right now defines much of spacecraft design and accelerate the transition toward an in-space circular economy,” Mitchell indicates.

In a recent development, can we do in space what we’ve failed to do on Earth? Right now, researchers are gathering data as fast as they can, as fast as resourcing allows, to inform models of ablation and atmospheric processes that will eventually be validated by measurements taken during reentry.

Then, equipped with actionable data, we can act.

Brain scans reveal where fractions fit on the mental number line

📅 21 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (1087 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Earth

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Brain scans show that adults use a shared mental number line to compare fractions and whole numbers, even as the brain distinguishes between them.
  • A quarter looks more like four on the page, but its value is much closer to zero.
  • As adults compared fractions and whole numbers, brain activity followed a shared number line.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Brain scans show that adults use a shared mental number line to compare fractions and whole numbers, even as the brain distinguishes between them.

A quarter looks more like four on the page, but its value is much closer to zero. In a upcoming brain scan study, that difference mattered.

As adults compared fractions and whole numbers, brain activity followed a shared number line.

The patterns still distinguished fractions from whole numbers, but numbers close in value tended to produce more similar patterns.

One idea about how the brain handles abstract concepts is that it files related concepts close together, so that similar ideas produce similar patterns of activity.

Numbers are a good way to test that, because everyone agrees on their order.

Daniela Valério and Stanislas Dehaene of the Inserm-CEA Cognitive Neuroimaging Unit, known as Unicog, led the study at the NeuroSpin center outside Paris.

People have long been known to carry a number line in their heads for whole numbers. The team wanted to know whether fractions, which children learn after years of schooling, get added to the same line.

Twenty-two adults took part, all right-handed native French speakers between 19 and 39 who had finished high school with a science track.

Two were excluded, one for a cyst found on the scan and one who had a panic attack in the scanner.

In a recent development, that left 20 participants in the brain scan analysis. A faulty response button reduced the number to 19 for the analysis of speed and accuracy.

In a recent development, each person lay in a high-field MRI scanner run by the French research agency CEA. The numbers 0, 1, 2, 3, 4, and 5 and the fractions 1/4, 1/3, 1/2, 2/3, 3/2, and 5/2 flashed up one at a time, each for one second.

For every number, the person pressed a button to say whether it was bigger or smaller than the one before.

Industry observers note that each run lasted just under ten minutes, and every number followed every other number exactly once. The fractions were built from the same digits as the whole numbers on purpose.

That let the team tell whether the brain was reading 1/4 as a quarter or as a 1 next to a 4.

It has been revealed that fractions slowed people down. A comparison between two fractions took about 1.2 seconds on average, against 0.8 seconds between two whole numbers.

People also got 9.5 percent of fraction pairs wrong, compared with 3.7 percent of whole number pairs.

In an interview with Earth.com, Valério said fractions are harder for a few reasons.

Whole numbers follow a simple counting sequence, so 3 is followed by 4, while there is always another fraction between any two different numbers.

According to recent reports, the size of a fraction is also not always easy to judge from the numbers in it. “For example, although 5 is greater than 3, 1/5 is smaller than 1/3,” Valério mentioned.

Industry observers note that numbers that were close together were also harder than numbers far apart, whichever kind they were. The closer two numbers were, the slower and less accurate people got, and the effect was strongest when both were fractions.

Psychologists have known this distance effect for whole numbers for decades, and here it held for fractions too.

The team then laid out the speed and error data as a map. The 12 numbers fell along a single curved line in order of size, with the fractions among the whole numbers where their values belonged.

Sources indicate that the scans demonstrated the same thing. Across the brain regions that handle math, the pattern of activity for each number varied along two main directions.

In a recent development, one separated fractions from whole numbers. The other ordered all 12 numbers by size, from small to large, and ignored whether they were fractions.

The size ordering was strongest in the intraparietal sulcus, a fold near the top and back of the brain that has long been tied to math.

According to recent reports, researchers have also linked this region to the ability to estimate quantities. In the latest study, patterns of activity in the hippocampus also reflected how close numbers were in value.

Then the team looked at single points on the cortex.

It has been revealed that within the front part of that parietal fold, many spots responded most to one particular number and less to its neighbors. The spots formed a map, with small numbers at the front and larger numbers farther back.

The map for fractions matched the map for whole numbers. Spots that preferred 0 also responded to 1/4, 1/3, and 1/2, and 1/4 ended up far from 4.

Valério remarked that when people compare numbers, they have to focus on magnitude, meaning how large or small each one is.

“Our study demonstrates that the brain organizes this information into a shared map, much like a mental number line, “Valerio told Earth.com.

“This map brings whole numbers, such as 1 and 2, and fractions, such as 1/2 and 2/3, into the same system, according to their values.”.

The size map showed up in only 14 or 15 of the 20 participants, depending on the number type. The fractions also stopped at 5/2, short of the range the whole numbers covered.

Fractions and whole numbers were mixed in one stream, so people may have had to build a single line to keep up.

The authors wrote that if the two kinds had been shown in separate sessions, each might still have run from small to large. The two lines might not have lined up, though.

Recent findings suggest that valério said the study was not designed to explain why fractions are harder to learn or to find the best way to teach them. Other studies in her lab are working on that.

Her next step is to see how the shared map differs across people with different mathematical backgrounds and levels of education, and whether those differences go with mathematical ability.

How the brain represents fractions in children who are still learning them remains an open question.

In a recent development, the team has posted its data and code on the Open Science Framework. It wrote that longer scanning sessions could extend the map to more kinds of math.

The full study was published in the journal PLOS Biology.

It has been revealed that A group of visitors walks past the Capitol on Sept. 22. (Bill Clark/CQ Roll Call file photo).

With stopgap funding set to expire in less than a month, Senate Republican appropriators Thursday unveiled a roughly $5.3 billion draft fiscal 2027 Legislative Branch spending bill that would boost security funding and sidestep contentious debates over a key watchdog.

The proposal would provide $965 million for Capitol Police, a nearly $83 million hike from fiscal 2026, but still short of the more than $1 billion the department requested as threats against lawmakers rise.

In a recent development, and it would bump funding for the Government Accountability Office up to $860 million, an increase of nearly 6 percent from fiscal 2026. That stands in contrast to the version of the bill advanced by the House Appropriations Committee in May, which floated slashing the GAO by 25 percent.

It joins several other draft spending bills released this week by Senate Appropriations Chair Susan Collins, R-Maine, who is trying to kickstart bicameral negotiations as lawmakers stare down a Dec. 11 deadline to fund the government.

Her committee ran into a stalemate on topline numbers earlier this year that stopped it from marking up any of the 12 annual bills, but lawmakers nipped the threat of a government shutdown in the bud ahead of the midterm elections by pushing through a continuing resolution. With that funding now set to expire next month, appropriators are hoping they can wrap up at least some of the bills while punting the rest into the next Congress with another stopgap.

Recent findings suggest that the Legislative Branch bill is the smallest of the 12 appropriations bills and typically among the least controversial. But debates over the GAO have become a sticking point during the Trump administration as the agency accuses the White House of violating budget laws — a move the Office of Management and Budget has pushed back on, arguing the GAO has no authority over the administration since it is part of the legislative branch.

Industry observers note that the GAO has been without a permanent head after its longtime leader Gene L. Dodaro retired last year, although Republicans are now making a last-ditch effort to get one confirmed during the lame-duck session before Democrats take power.

The House version of the spending bill sought to bar the comptroller general from suing under the 1974 budget law restricting presidential impoundments, unless specifically authorized by Congress. But the Senate proposal includes no such language, and overall, it appears designed to avoid drastic or contentious moves.

It would also leave in place a provision that would block cost-of-living adjustments for members of Congress, whose pay has been frozen since 2009.

Senate Democrats, however, criticized the bill text after its release, saying it wouldn’t invest enough in the legislative branch.

“The Legislative Branch bill underfunds key work to support oversight of the Executive Branch, and it underfunds vital efforts to keep the Capitol complex safe,” Senate Appropriations ranking member Patty Murray, D-Wash., noted in a statement.

The Architect of the Capitol would get $762.5 million, though funding for House office buildings is not included in that total. The agency is requesting $1.6 billion as it seeks to begin large-scale renovations of the Rayburn House Office Building. The architect has repeatedly warned lawmakers that parts of the Capitol complex are in need of critical infrastructure upgrades, arguing that delaying renovations will only make them more expensive as things continue to deteriorate.

The bill’s $5.3 billion proposal represents funding for the Senate and legislative branch agencies, while excluding House-only funds, which are typically added later.

According to Whynter, the inverter technology delivers 20 percent more cooling capacity and over 40 percent energy savings compared to non-inverter models. Do note, though, that while this is technically a portable unit, at more than 75 pounds, it’s one you’ll want to set up for the season, not haul around on the regular.

In a recent development, if you're shopping for a portable AC because you have a room your HVAC system can’t handle, the Midea Duo MAP14HS1TBL is our top recommendation. It's a four-season unit: the same inverter-driven, hose-in-hose dual-hose design that makes it such an effective cooler works equally well in heat mode, and switching between the two is as easy as a click on the remote or SmartHome app—no setup or adjustments required.

Recent findings suggest that the dual-hose design pulls in fresh air and expels exhaust air through a single concentric hose, keeping a neutral pressure balance in rooms. This prevents warm outside air from coming back in through gaps and cracks. Midea's airflow system also projects air up to 26 feet, which makes a real difference in longer rooms where less forceful units only cool the area immediately around them.

We’re also impressed by the smart controls. The SmartHome app works on iOS, Android, and Apple Watch, and voice control is compatible with Alexa and Google Assistant. I also like that you can completely turn off the control panel lights, which is a sleep-saving feature for overnight use. And at 42 decibels on its lowest setting, it's among the quietest options we’ve come across.

Recent findings suggest that we were pleasantly surprised by the power and value offered by this small portable air conditioner from Black+Decker. It begins producing cold air very rapidly, though not quite at the volume of many other air conditioners we tested. That remarked, it still reduced the temperature of its target at a rapid rate.

In a recent development, the unit provides multiple fan speeds, dedicated dehumidification, a timer setting, and a sleep setting. Note that there is no heater setting on this appliance. It’s meant to cool and dehumidify exclusively.

Recent findings suggest that reviews Editor Amber Joglar tested out the four-in-one version of this model which also functions as a heater. After just 10 minutes of use in her room, Joglar felt, “a noticeable shift in the air temperature.”.

It has been revealed that the quick cooldown times stood out across both models, though Joglar also pointed out that this led to the exhaust pipes heating up swiftly as well. This isn’t necessarily a problem, but if you proposal on using the unit for several hours a day, consider covering the tubes in insulation.

In addition to the cold air, Joglar liked the remote and LED control panel, saying, “I normally just change settings on the air conditioner itself because it’s right next to my bed, so backlit controls are helpful.”.

Similarly, the remote control is great for when she’s already in bed or wants to pre-cool the room before she’s ready to go to sleep.

According to recent reports, joglar’s model also heats rooms. So, instead of storing it in a closet or attic for the cold winter months, she simply switches functionality.

Read Our Full Black+Decker Portable Air Conditioner Review.

Coverage area is one of the most important factors in choosing an air conditioner. Manufacturers rate units in square footage, but that number assumes an average ceiling height (roughly eight feet) and room insulation. If the room is especially hot in the summer (for example, it’s a finished attic or it has large, south-facing windows) we recommend bumping up to the next size rather than buying a unit that will run constantly and struggle to keep up.

It has been revealed that an air conditioner’s cooling capacity is typically measured in British Thermal Units, or BTU, per hour. To gauge coverage, figure roughly 20 BTU per square foot of space. Most portable a/c units range from 5,000 to 20,000 BTUs, which puts their effective range roughly between 350 and 700 square feet. So when in doubt, size up—an oversized unit cycles off when it hits your target temperature, while an undersized one never stops trying.

Recent findings suggest that single-hose units essentially recirculate the room’s air to cool it and have one line that runs outdoors to expel exhaust. The catch is that expelling air creates a slight negative pressure in the room, which pulls in warm air from other parts of the house and from outside through gaps around doors and windows. It works, but it’s working against itself.

It has been revealed that dual-hose units solve this by pulling outside air in through one hose for cooling and pushing hot exhaust out through a second hose. The result is a more self-contained system that’s noticeably more efficient, especially in larger spaces. The tradeoff is price.

In a recent development, because dual-hose models are more complex, they tend to be more expensive. If you only have a small space to cool, a portable a/c with a single hose may suit your needs just fine. For anything larger, the dual-hose design is worth seriously considering.

Recent findings suggest that hose length determines how far away from a window you can maneuver your portable air conditioner. If you set it up in a large room, or one where the nearest window is far from where most people gather, hose length becomes more important.

In a recent development, it also plays a key role in room setup. If the hose isn’t long enough to set the air conditioner in front of large furniture pieces, you may have to rearrange the room for the most effective cooling. Most hoses range anywhere from 50 to 90 inches fully extended. This should give you enough space to make adjustments and pull the air conditioner closer to the center of the room if needed.

Most portable air conditioners hover between 50 and 60 decibels while they’re running—that’s roughly the noise level of a normal conversation. In most cases, that’s fine during the day, but if you’re planning to run the unit in a bedroom overnight, those numbers start to matter.

Recent findings suggest that units that dip below 50 decibels in their quietest modes are on par with most ceiling fans and are easier to sleep through; a few on this list get impressively close to whisper-quiet. Pay attention to the decibel rating at the unit’s lowest fan setting, not just its average operating level.

Sources indicate that much like larger ductless mini-split air conditioners, some portable air conditioners include a heat pump. “If you’re shopping for an a/c unit because you have a space not currently cooled or heated, one of these models may warrant consideration,” notes gear editor Bradley Ford. “Similarly, you may have a room that your HVAC system doesn’t reach effectively. Rooms like this are typically either too cold or hot, depending on the season. If this is the case, a unit with heating capabilities may be able to fill your HVAC gap.”.

It has been revealed that every portable a/c pulls moisture out of the air, similar to home dehumidifiers. The question is what happens to it next. Budget units collect it in an internal pan that you’ll need to manually drain, sometimes daily in humid conditions.

It has been revealed that other units use self-evaporating technology to push moisture out through the exhaust hose with no bucket to remember. A few high-end models go even further, offering a continuous drainage port where you can attach a hose and never think about water again. If low-maintenance matters to you, the drainage method is a factor to consider.

According to recent reports, there isn’t a clear superior option between window units and portable options. Choosing between the two largely depends on your home, windows, and personal needs. That said, window air conditioning units are generally faster at bringing temperatures down and run more efficiently than their portable counterparts.

Portable air conditioners have certainly closed the gap over time in terms of cooling ability, but still lag behind if that’s your number one priority.

Sources indicate that portable units stand out because of their convenience and ease of setup. If you don’t have compatible windows, get a portable unit. If you need quick cooling in a spot that generally doesn’t need air conditioning, get a portable unit. If you want just one machine for your entire apartment, get a portable unit.

Portable air conditioners are compatible with a lot more window openings than window units, so you can use them regardless of your apartment or home fixtures.

New portable a/c units are relatively energy efficient across the board. That mentioned, it’s certainly a sliding scale. There are several ways in which energy efficiency is calculated for air conditioners, but the shorthand is if your a/c unit is Energy Star-certified, it’s worth getting.

For items that don’t have Energy Star certification, pay attention to the CEER, EER, and SEER numbers. In short, look for an air conditioner with a CEER above 10, with anything above 12 qualifying for Energy Star certification. Similarly, look out for a SEER above 14 in the north and 15 in the south as well as an EER above 10. These are general numbers, but serve as a basic guide when choosing between different options.

Industry observers note that one of the biggest complications to solve with portable air conditioners is cooling efficiency. While most units generate a ton of cold air, leakage from the hose or exhaust port can work against that. There are two key things you can do: insulate the opening in the window and insulate the hose itself.

Many portable units provide foam pieces that fit in and around the window insert to minimize the amount of hot air that leaks in from outside. The hose itself won’t come with foam insulation pieces, but you can perform a similar trick by buying one online or by making one yourself. Some people use blankets while others have used everything from reflective sun shades to Amazon plastic packaging. The goal is to prevent heat from the tube from radiating into your living space.

#42838. Hawaii’s 90-foot Hōlei Sea Arch was carved from lava that flowed about 550 years ago, and in late September it fell into the Pacific

Hawaii’s 90-foot Hōlei Sea Arch was carved from lava that flowed about 550 years ago, and in late September it fell into the Pacific

📅 21 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (794 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Earth

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • The 90-foot Hōlei Sea Arch in Hawaiʻi Volcanoes National Park collapsed in late September 2026.
  • For years, visitors who drove to the end of Chain of Craters Road in Hawaiʻi Volcanoes National Park could walk a short distance and see a 90-foot arch of lava rock reaching out from the cliffs into the Pacific Ocean.
  • In a recent development, that view is gone.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

The 90-foot Hōlei Sea Arch in Hawaiʻi Volcanoes National Park collapsed in late September 2026. Here is how it formed and why sea arches eventually fall.

For years, visitors who drove to the end of Chain of Craters Road in Hawaiʻi Volcanoes National Park could walk a short distance and see a 90-foot arch of lava rock reaching out from the cliffs into the Pacific Ocean.

In a recent development, that view is gone. The Hōlei Sea Arch was still standing on Wednesday, September 23, 2026. By the night of Sunday, September 27, it had collapsed into the ocean, the National Park Service revealed on October 1.

The exact time of the collapse is unknown. According to the park, it could have happened while the park was temporarily closed during Tropical Storm Nolo.

The arch stood about 90 feet (27.4 meters) high and extended from steep sea cliffs into the ocean along the park’s southern coast, on the Island of Hawaiʻi.

It was carved into the cliff of an ancient lava flow from about 550 years ago, according to the park. The arch took shape through what geologists call differential erosion: some layers of lava are harder than others, so the sea wears them away at different speeds.

Visitors could see it by walking a short distance from the end of Chain of Craters Road, which the park described in 2020 as a 19-mile drive through some of the most spectacular scenery in the park.

The park’s own page on the arch was clear about one thing. The formation was beautiful but temporary, with a limited life span, and it would eventually crumble into the sea.

Sources indicate that sea arches like Hōlei can be found along a wide stretch of Hawaiʻi’s southern coast. They are remnants of once-continuous sea cliffs, built where lava met the sea and added to the size of the island.

Lava meeting the sea can even build whole new land, as it did when a new island rose from the sea off Iceland in 1963.

Recent findings suggest that the moment that new lava cooled and turned to rock, it began to erode, the park explains. The seas on the island’s southern edge are known for rough water and violent surf, and the waves slowly break apart the rock and carve sea caves into the cliffs.

In a recent development, when waves hit the back wall of a sea cave, the water bounces back and starts to erode the cave’s headland. Over time, that forms an arch.

The erosion does not stop there. Given enough time, the waves cause the remaining bridge of rock to collapse, leaving behind a pile of rocks known as a sea stack.

Volcanic coastlines are constantly being remade, and on the same island, Kīlauea has produced 55 lava fountains since December 2024.

The coastline around the arch had shown signs of instability for years.

Earthquakes during the 2018 Kīlauea eruption and summit collapse damaged the cliffs near the arch. In January 2020, new cracks and instability led the park to close the original viewing area and the short trail to it.

“This latest development reminds us that Hawaiʻi Volcanoes National Park is an ever-changing volcanic landscape,” Rhonda Loh, then the park’s acting superintendent, stated in January 2020.

A safer viewing area opened in March 2020, about 1,000 feet past the gate at the end of Chain of Craters Road and set back from the cliff edge.

Later that year, massive surf from Tropical Storm Darby broke off a chunk of rock from the lower part of the arch.

The park is urging visitors to stay back from the unstable cliffs, which drop vertically into the ocean and present a serious risk of falling.

After the collapse, photos on social media showed people entering the closed area near where the arch once stood.

According to the park, that puts both the visitors and first responders at great risk of falling and drowning off the rough, wave-swept coast.

Visitors are required to stay out of closed areas and away from cliff edges, which can collapse without warning.

The park describes individual sea arches as an ephemeral feature of the island’s constantly shifting coastline.

It has been revealed that as the cliff slowly migrates inland, other arches will form and replace Hōlei, the park states. The park notes that erosion does not stop once an arch has formed.

The information was obtained from the National Park Service’s announcement of the collapse, its pages on Hōlei Sea Arch and how sea arches form, and its 2020 releases on the closure of the overlook and the new viewing area.

Tech Report: The Sky This Week from November 20 to 27: Uranus at opposition
