💡 Key Takeaways
  • According to recent reports, friday, November 20The Moon passes 5° north of Neptune at 8 A.M.
  • Sources indicate that in the northeast, Auriga the Charioteer is above the horizon by 7 P.M.
  • According to recent reports, why are these called the Kids?
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

According to recent reports, friday, November 20The Moon passes 5° north of Neptune at 8 A.M. EST, then passes 7° north of Saturn at 8 P.M. EST. They remain visible all evening, forming a triangle in southern Pisces and northern Cetus. The Moon and Saturn are visible to the naked eye, but Neptune will be invisible without binoculars or a telescope. Check out last week’s column for more details on how to view the celestial trio.

Sources indicate that in the northeast, Auriga the Charioteer is above the horizon by 7 P.M. local time. Its brightest star is Capella, which shines at magnitude 0.1 and sits some 43 light-years away. Just southeast of this star, you’ll find another triangle in the sky tonight. This small shape is an asterism about 2.7° long, known as the Kids. It consists of Epsilon (ε), Zeta (ζ), and Eta (η) Aurigae, which range from 3rd (Epsilon and Eta) to 4th (Zeta) magnitude.

According to recent reports, why are these called the Kids? Capella’s name essentially means “She-Goat,” according to the late stellar expert Jim Kaler. These fainter stars cluster close by the brighter star like goat kids around their mother.

According to recent reports, mercury reaches greatest western elongation (20°) at 7 P.M. EST; it will be visible before dawn tomorrow morning, so keep reading for more details.

Sources indicate that sunrise: 6:51 A.M. Sunset: 4:40 P.M. Moonrise: 2:04 P.M. Moonset: 2:12 A.M. Moon Phase: Waxing gibbous (84%) *Times for sunrise, sunset, moonrise, and moonset are given in local time from 40° N 90° W. The Moon’s illumination is given at 10 P.M. local time from the same location.

Recent findings suggest that saturday, November 21If you’ve got a viewing site with a clear eastern horizon, this morning offers a great opportunity to spot the solar system’s innermost planet. Look for Mercury about an hour before sunrise, when it reaches 7° high and shines at magnitude –0.5. The planet reached its greatest western elongation from our Sun yesterday evening, and is now 20° west of our star in the sky.

In a recent development, located in Libra, the tiny world sits to the far lower left of bright Venus, higher in the sky. Venus is in the constellation Virgo, standing just north (to the upper left) of the bright star Spica. Another bright star, Arcturus in Boötes, hangs to that pair’s far upper left.

Pull out a telescope to check out the size and phase of each planet. Start with Venus, whose disk spans a hefty 46” — presently larger than Jupiter’s apparent size in our sky. Despite its impressive width, however, the disk of Venus appears as just a sliver, only 19% lit. Slide down to Mercury for comparison, and see that its phase is much larger — 62% — while the planet’s overall apparent width is much smaller, just 7”.

Sources indicate that if you’re able, keep watching Mercury day by day in the morning sky. Its gibbous phase will continue growing, reaching 84% lit by the end of the month.

Sources indicate that sunrise: 6:52 A.M. Sunset: 4:39 P.M. Moonrise: 2:29 P.M. Moonset: 3:22 A.M. Moon Phase: Waxing gibbous (92%).

Sources indicate that sunday, November 22With the Moon not far from Full, its western limb is now coming into view as the Sun rises across the lunar landscape. The large, flat-floored crater Schickard is prominent in the southwest, near the small, circular Mare Humorum. Because the nearly Full Moon is so bright, you may want to use a Moon filter before you turn your telescope toward our satellite tonight for a closer look.

According to recent reports, zoom in on Schickard to discover that its dark floor isn’t perfectly smooth, but pockmarked by smaller craters that came after the initial, larger crater’s formation. Its outer walls are shallow and beaten down, also showing off their age. Look closely at Schickard’s western wall to see how it has slumped, particularly compared to the eastern side of the crater rim. Also compare the texture of the southwestern portion of the crater floor, which appears quite rough, to the rest of the crater, which is smoother. The difference arises because most of the crater was flooded by lava, which didn’t quite reach its southwestern regions.

Stretching about 130 miles (210 kilometers) across, Schickard is roughly 4 billion years old and was formed by a giant impact. Because it sits so near the limb of the Moon, it often looks oblong from our vantage point on Earth — but from above, orbiters have shown it is really quite circular in shape.

Sunrise: 6:53 A.M. Sunset: 4:39 P.M. Moonrise: 2:59 P.M. Moonset: 4:34 A.M. Moon Phase: Waxing gibbous (97%).

In a recent development, monday, November 23A few hours after sunset, the house-shaped constellation Cepheus stands on the point of its roof in the northern sky, above the Little Dipper. Cepheus is home to several lovely double stars, including Xi (ξ) Cephei, also known as Kurhah.

Glowing at magnitude 4.3, Kurhah is not one of the stars in the house’s outline, but lies within the boxy base. You can find it about midway between Alderamin (Alpha [α] Cep) and Iota (ι) Cep, the western and eastern points in the house’s box, respectively. Kurhah’s two components are separated by just under 8” — once you find the star in binoculars or your finder scope, any telescope will split them. The pair consists of a brighter magnitude 4.4 primary, which glows white, and a fainter magnitude 6.5 secondary, which appears to many observers as yellow.

It has been revealed that if you happen to have a large telescope, you may want to give a nearby deep-sky treasure a try: planetary nebula NGC 7139 sits just 2° west-southwest of Kurhah, but it requires a large scope (8 inches at least) to spot, as this bubble of gas glows at magnitude 13.3. If available, an Oxygen-III filter will help bring it out by dimming the nearby stars.

It has been revealed that sunrise: 6:54 A.M. Sunset: 4:38 P.M. Moonrise: 3:37 P.M. Moonset: 5:52 A.M. Moon Phase: Full.

According to recent reports, tuesday, November 24Full Moon occurs at 9:54 A.M. EST, bringing us our second Super Moon of the year. A Super Moon occurs when the Moon reaches Full phase close to perigee, its closest point to Earth, making our satellite appear larger and brighter than average. The November Full Moon is also called the Beaver Moon.

Industry observers note that A few hours earlier, before dawn, the Full Moon passes through the Pleiades star cluster (M45) in Taurus, occulting several of its bright stars. This is an easy event to watch, visible to the naked eye — or you can get a closer view with binoculars or a telescope (just note that you may want a Moon filter if available, as our satellite is so big and bright). The timing of the event will depend heavily on your location; note that it begins right around sunrise along the East Coast, so observers there may only see the Moon approaching the famous group of stars.

The 5th-magnitude star Celaeno (16 Tauri) disappears behind the Moon’s leading edge just moments before 6 A.M. CST, followed minutes later by 4th-magnitude Taygeta (19 Tau). Next to vanish is 4th-magnitude Maia (20 Tau) just before 6:20 A.M. CST, followed quickly by Sterope (21 Tau) a few minutes later. The latter two may be difficult to catch from the Midwest without optical aid, as sunrise is fast approaching. If you are using binoculars or a telescope in this region, make sure to put them away several minutes ahead of sunrise from your location. Celaeno reappears around 6:40 A.M. CST, 15 minutes or so before sunrise.

For specific timings from your location, visit the International Occultation Timing Association at http://www.lunar-occultations.com/bobgraze/index.html.

Recent findings suggest that the Moon then passes 5° north of Uranus (also in Taurus) at 2 P.M. EST. Over in the constellation Leo, Mars passes 1.8° north of Regulus at 5 P.M. EST.

Sunrise: 6:55 A.M. Sunset: 4:38 P.M. Moonrise: 4:24 P.M. Moonset: 7:10 A.M. Moon Phase: Waning gibbous (99%).

Recent findings suggest that wednesday, November 25The Moon reaches perigee, the closest point to Earth in its orbit, at 4:01 P.M. EST. At that time, our satellite will stand 223,288 miles (359,347 km) away.

The distant ice giant Uranus reaches opposition tonight at 6 P.M. EST. Opposition is the best time to view a planet in our sky, and it’s visible roughly from dusk until dawn. Because Uranus is faint — magnitude 5.6 — you’ll want to give it a few hours after sunset to climb away from both light pollution and turbulent air near the horizon. Around 10 P.M. local time, you’ll find Uranus midway between the bright star Aldebaran and the Pleiades star cluster in Taurus the Bull, about 60° above the southeastern horizon. It sits some 1.5° south of 4th-magnitude 37 Tauri.

In a recent development, although Uranus can be visible to the naked eye under clear, dark conditions, the bright waning Moon is nearby, so pull out binoculars or a telescope to view the far-off planet tonight. Once you land on its location, look for a “flat,” grayish-colored star. Uranus’ disk spans 4”, so you will likely be able to tell it is circular, rather than a pinpoint of light like any background stars.

Sources indicate that sunrise: 6:56 A.M. Sunset: 4:37 P.M. Moonrise: 5:24 P.M. Moonset: 8:26 A.M. Moon Phase: Waning gibbous (96%).

Recent findings suggest that thursday, November 26Celebrate Thanksgiving with a celestial turkey: The famous Orion Nebula (M42) is also playfully known as the Turkey Nebula because it looks to some like a turkey, particularly in deep astrophotos. But whether you’re a photographer or not, this bright deep-sky treat is easy to enjoy tonight while dinner digests.

According to recent reports, by about 9 P.M. local time, Orion the Hunter has risen above the eastern horizon, his recognizable three-star belt standing in a vertical line. The lowest star in that line is Alnitak (Zeta [ζ] Orionis), and the Orion Nebula lies just 3.7° south-southwest of this star, to its lower right on the sky this evening. You might be able to spot its glow without optical aid, although the bright Moon nearby may make that difficult. Binoculars or any telescope will easily show it.

At 4th magnitude and spanning some 85’ by 60’, the Orion Nebula is a huge and bright star-forming region that sits roughly 1,350 light-years from Earth. In the brightest portion of the nebula lies a small grouping of young stars called the Trapezium Cluster. Take your time with this gorgeous sight, scanning around the region to pick out detail in the nebulosity. And if you are an astrophotographer, consider turning the view into a Thanksgiving memory to share for years to come.

In a recent development, sunrise: 6:58 A.M. Sunset: 4:37 P.M. Moonrise: 6:35 P.M. Moonset: 9:33 A.M. Moon Phase: Waning gibbous (91%).

Friday, November 27The Moon-free window for observing Comet 161P/Hartley-IRAS reopens tonight, the same day the comet reaches perihelion, the closest point to the Sun in its 21½-year orbit. It has been a fairly stable 10th to 11th magnitude, and although it has no appreciable tail, the nucleus’ green glow has been notable in recent astrophotos.

Recent findings suggest that you’ll find Hartley-IRAS in the west a few hours after sunset. Around 7 P.M. local time it is still 30° high, well above the turbulent air near the ground that can muddy astronomical views. Tonight the comet is in western Sagitta, about 6.3° north-northeast of 3rd-magnitude Zeta (ζ) Aquilae. Even a small (4-inch) scope will net you a view, but larger apertures will show more detail around the nucleus, allowing you to look for features such as a sharpened southern flank as it flies into the solar headwind.

In a recent development, while you’re in this region, make sure to sweep just 2.1° northeast of the comet’s location to spot the famous Coathanger asterism in Vulpecula. This 1°-long grouping of stars looks just like its namesake, with the hook on the southern side of the hanger’s arms.

According to recent reports, sunrise: 6:59 A.M. Sunset: 4:36 P.M. Moonrise: 7:53 P.M. Moonset: 10:26 A.M. Moon Phase: Waning gibbous (82%).

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Fish and Wildlife Service crew caught a rare yellow burbot in Oswego Harbor, Fresh York.

  • The agency calls it a one-in-a-million catch.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

A U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service crew caught a rare yellow burbot in Oswego Harbor, Fresh York. A genetic condition gave it the color, and it went to Cornell.

According to recent reports, biologists with the U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service were running a routine survey in Oswego Harbor, Newly introduced York, on Lake Ontario, in October when they pulled up a fish they did not expect. It was a burbot, and it was bright yellow-orange.

The agency calls it a one-in-a-million catch. The fish has xanthochromism, a rare condition that gives it a saturated yellow-orange color.

The agency said the fish would make even the brightest fall foliage look pale in comparison.

It is also the first burbot ever documented during a fisheries survey in Oswego Harbor, although a few anglers have reported catching them there.

Xanthochromism is caused by a genetic mutation that suppresses normal pigmentation and produces the yellow-orange appearance.

According to recent reports, it is considerably less common in wild fish than albinism or melanism, according to the Fish and Wildlife Service. Unusual colors like this have surprised scientists before, as with a bright orange shark.

Industry observers note that the place was a surprise too. Burbot populations in the lake are extremely low, and the species usually lives in deeper, cooler water than what is found inside the harbor.

According to recent reports, the crew was not looking for burbot. It came from the Lower Great Lakes Fish and Wildlife Conservation Office, and it was carrying out an Aquatic Invasive Species survey.

The program watches harbors, rivers and bays of the Great Lakes for invasive species on a watchlist.

Because invaders are often rare when they first arrive, the crews use several methods at once, including electrofishing, fyke nets, gill nets and environmental DNA, or eDNA.

Invaders are an old problem in these waters: the Great Lakes have been under invasion from one species for 70 years.

Most fish caught in these surveys are native species. Catching a rare native fish suggests the program may also detect newly arriving invaders when their numbers are still very low.

The agency summed it up as an effective survey strategy, along with a bit of luck.

The burbot is a native fish of the Great Lakes. It tends to live on the lake bottom, and it is the only cod-like fish species in freshwater, according to a Latest York Sea Grant fact sheet. The same fact sheet calls it a formidable predator.

In the Great Lakes, sea lamprey predation has been a common factor affecting burbot numbers.

Sources indicate that A 2006 study led by U.S. Geological Survey scientists found that burbot abundance in eastern Lake Erie increased significantly between 1987 and 2003.

The researchers, writing in Transactions of the American Fisheries Society, attributed the apparent recovery to effective sea lamprey control.

The same study suggested that a relatively high density of alewives, a small plankton-eating fish, probably held burbot numbers down in Lakes Ontario and Michigan at the time.

When U.S. Geological Survey fisheries biologists who know the species processed the yellow burbot, they noticed it was emaciated and looked to be in poor health.

Because of its condition, and because the reasons the species remains so scarce in the lake are still unexplained, the fish was sent to the Cornell University College of Veterinary Medicine for a health analysis. The agency has not reported the results.

The agency claims the catch could turn out to be lucky for the species too.

The rare fish may offer valuable insight into the health of burbot populations across the basin, and that could help guide how they are managed.

The information was obtained from the U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service, a Newly introduced York Sea Grant fact sheet and a U.S. Geological Survey study.

A peanut by a lamp can make a city crow warier than a passing human

📅 21 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1229 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Earth

⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • With a lamp base beside the peanuts, feeding odds fell to 0.53 for city crows and 0.76 for country crows in a Binghamton study of 20 crow families.
  • In 2019 and 2020, a team led by biologist Dave J.
  • On some mornings the peanuts had manufacturer: a rock, an ear of corn in its husk, a paper takeout box or a faux-wood lamp base.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

With a lamp base beside the peanuts, feeding odds fell to 0.53 for city crows and 0.76 for country crows in a Binghamton study of 20 crow families.

In 2019 and 2020, a team led by biologist Dave J. Colucci put out peanuts in the shell for 20 families of American crows around Ithaca, Newly introduced York. Ten families lived in town, and ten in farm fields and natural areas of the nearby Town of Dryden.

On some mornings the peanuts had manufacturer: a rock, an ear of corn in its husk, a paper takeout box or a faux-wood lamp base. Country crows held back more around the box, and city crows around the corn.

Sources indicate that city crows were also less likely to eat next to the lamp, the study by Colucci and Anne Clark of Binghamton University found. Other urban-rural differences in the paper had only weak support.

It has been revealed that colucci earned a PhD at Binghamton in 2025. Clark is an associate professor emerita of biological sciences there, the Binghamton University release of November 16, 2026, says. The paper came out online in Behavioral Ecology on October 22.

Each family’s territory got a feeding spot. The bait was 2 cups of raw, unsalted peanuts in a circle about 3 feet (1 meter) wide. They picked spots with little human traffic and no sign of predators or competitors.

In town these were parking lots, dead-end streets and parks in Ithaca, Lansing and Cayuga Heights. Out in Dryden the sites were on private or public land.

Each family got three days with peanuts only and four days with an object, 140 trials in total, each starting between 6 and 8 a.m.

A hidden camcorder sat at least 10 feet (3 meters) from the bait. The observer stayed 164 feet (50 meters) or more away.

The team ranked the objects by how often a crow in each place would have seen them. Rocks are everywhere and corn grows in Dryden, while takeout boxes are more common in town.

“What we wanted to show was that aversion would decrease with the amount of experience that we expected our crow to have had with these objects,” Colucci remarked in the release.

According to recent reports, to test the trash part, the team surveyed a 1-mile (1.61-kilometer) road route in each area weekly for three weeks. They counted 341 human-made objects, 169 in town and 172 in the country. Rural ones stayed put longer, 2.81 weeks on average against 2.27.

Recent findings suggest that the box cut feeding more for rural crows and the corn cut it more for urban crows. But the paper says the evidence for that switch was limited.

Sources indicate that crows that live near an Arby’s or a McDonald’s learn to recognize that chain’s boxes, Clark said in the release. The box in the test was a plain one with no brand.

The lamp base was supposed to be new to every crow, in town or out. The authors chose it because it has none of the usual signs of a human-made thing, like bright colors, shine or sharp corners.

Industry observers note that with peanuts alone, nearly every visit ended in feeding, a probability of 0.99 in town and 0.97 in Dryden. Put the lamp down and it fell to 0.53 for urban crows and 0.76 for rural crows, according to the paper’s Bayesian model.

Sources indicate that how fast the birds came in was another matter. Timing for the boldest crow in each family was about the same in both places with the lamp out. That held for reaching 10 feet (3 meters) of the bait and for taking a first peanut.

In a recent development, overall, the urban families did reach the bait sooner, at 4.23 times the rural rate. The authors attribute this to the rural crows partly reacting to the person on watch, since country crows are warier of people.

Earlier work had mostly found that city birds are bolder with new things, which is why the release calls this somewhat surprising. Clark stated urban crows “are social animals” that watch one another. “In an area that has a lot of new opportunities, there are also new threats,” she said.

According to recent reports, the second test was about people. An experimenter walked toward single crows and noted how close the walker got before each one flew, a figure biologists call flight initiation distance.

One person did all 145 trials, in upstate New York and in Quebec, in 2019, 2022 and 2023. The pace was a steady 2.7 miles per hour (1.2 meters per second). On some walks the experimenter looked at the crow, and on others tilted the whole face down.

Industry observers note that on average the crows took off when the walker was about 149 feet (45.3 meters) away. The walker got closer than 33 feet (10 meters) only 8 times. Where the walker looked mattered only in more crowded places.

The model looked at areas with about 13,000 people per square mile (5,000 per square kilometer). There, it put the distance for a downward look near zero, about 82 feet (25 meters) shorter than for a stare. Rural crows left at about the same distance either way.

Sources indicate that the authors warn that those predictions are uncertain. Human population within about half a mile (800 meters) of each trial predicted flight distance best.

Industry observers note that crow hunting is allowed in rural Latest York in a set season but prohibited within city limits, the paper notes. The release indicates crows, seen as a nuisance, are more likely to be shot in rural areas.

Clark called the rural behavior “a blunt, anti-predator strategy” in the release. “Whereas in urban areas, if you were fleeing at every human, you’d never spend any time on the ground,” she noted.

The authors compare the gaze result with earlier work on Seattle crows, where flight distance was on average about 10.5 feet (3.2 meters) shorter for an indirect gaze.

Separate University of Washington mask experiments found that wild crows learned the faces of dangerous people and passed the details to other crows. They remembered a threatening person for up to 17 years.

Separate lab work in Germany found carrion crows that made decisions about twice as fast as humans in a visual task.

Sources indicate that the town sites were really suburban, the authors say, not downtown. The litter count covered roadsides at one site per area, and the timing data on approaches came from 2020 only.

One person ran every flight trial, and the approach timings may partly reflect wariness of the experimenter. Census numbers may also miss parks and shopping areas, where few people live but many walk through.

The lamp may not have been fully new to city crows either. It is perfectly symmetrical around its vertical axis, a shape rare in nature and common in things people make. So the town-country gap could be underestimated, the paper says.

In Ithaca and Dryden, the 20 crow families got the same peanuts. What sat next to them, and who was walking by, changed what they did.

The full study was published in the journal Behavioral Ecology.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Looking for a sky event this week? Check out our full Sky This Week column.

November 19: Mercury moves into Libra.

The Moon passes 5° north of Neptune at 8 A.M. EST; 12 hours later, our satellite passes 7° north of Saturn at 8 P.M. EST. The trio is visible in the southeastern sky two hours after sunset, forming a triangle with the Moon to the upper left of Saturn, and Neptune to Saturn’s right. Only the Moon and Saturn are visible to the naked eye, while Neptune will require optical aid.

From the gibbous Moon, drop down first to check out Saturn through a telescope, including its lovely ring system and brightest moon, Titan. Saturn is the brightest object in this part of the sky after the Moon, so you don’t have to worry about misidentifying it. After passing south of the ringed world earlier this week, Titan now sits about 3.2’ to Saturn’s west, in line with the rings. Fainter moons Tethys, Rhea, and Dione may be visible clustered closer to the planet, but the bright moonlight might also make them challenging for visual observation.

From Saturn, scan 6.6° west-southwest to land on Neptune. If you have a go-to scope, it may take you right to the outermost planet, which glows at magnitude 7.7 and offers up a tiny, 2”-wide disk. It may look like a “flat,” bluish-gray star, rather than a bright pinprick of white light. Look for a large parallelogram of 4th- and 5th-magnitude stars just over 9° to Saturn’s southwest if you need a closer stepping stone. The star at the northeastern point of that shape is 5th-magnitude 29 Piscium, and it lies about 2.6° southwest of Neptune.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

This is a human-written story voiced by AI. Got feedback? Take our survey . (See our AI policy here .).

In a recent development, more U.S. women are taking menopause hormone therapy, fresh prescription data suggest.

Monthly dispensing of hormone therapy for women aged 40 to 74 more than doubled since 2023, growing from 2 million to 4.9 million, researchers report November 19 in JAMA. The analysis of U.S. pharmacy dispensing data revealed that this increase began in 2024. The rise continued in 2025, before and after the Food and Drug Administration’s November removal of the black box warning from packaging, and into 2026.

Although the data in the upcoming study are aggregate, the researchers used population data to estimate the dispensing rate for this age group, which jumped from 28 prescriptions per 1,000 women to 67 prescriptions per 1,000 over the period studied.

Industry observers note that the new study wasn’t designed to determine what’s behind the increase. It’s possible that the evidence regarding hormone therapy’s safety and effectiveness for the treatment of menopause symptoms, such as hot flashes, is reaching more women. Medical groups such as the Menopause Society have recommended menopause hormone therapy for women with symptoms who are younger than 60 or within 10 years of the start of menopause, absent certain risk factors including prior breast cancer and stroke.

“Greater attention to women’s health, updated medical guidance supporting individualized menopause hormone therapy and social media may all be contributing to increased interest,” claims Dana Sarnak, who studies sexual and reproductive health at Johns Hopkins School of Medicine. Anecdotally, her clinician colleagues report more patients seeking menopause care, she says.

According to recent reports, many women and physicians turned away from hormone therapy in the early 2000s after a large study called the Women’s Health Initiative raised safety concerns, which were later considered overblown. Research since then has provided a more nuanced understanding of the benefits and risks of menopause hormone therapy at different ages.

There are safer formulations, including patches and gels, of estrogen today then at the time of the Women’s Health Initiative, for which participants took a pill. The latest study found that product use increased for transdermal and vaginal estrogen and for progesterone products — women who have their uterus need to take progesterone along with estrogen. The use of oral formulations remained stable. There has been a shortage of estrogen patches in the United States this year, which the U.S. Food and Drug Administration attributes to increasing demand.

#42830. Fossil teeth challenge a long-held idea about where early humans could live

📅 21 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 6m • 📚 Deep Dive (1196 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Earth ↗ Open Full Page

Fossil teeth challenge a long-held idea about where early humans could live

📅 21 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1196 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Earth

⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Eight fossil teeth from two caves in southern China suggest that Homo erectus lived in rainforests and survived in the region longer than scientists thought.
  • Dense tropical rainforest was long regarded as a habitat that only our own species, Homo sapiens, had mastered.
  • In a recent development, homo erectus, an extinct human relative, spread from Africa across Asia.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Eight fossil teeth from two caves in southern China suggest that Homo erectus lived in rainforests and survived in the region longer than scientists thought.

Dense tropical rainforest was long regarded as a habitat that only our own species, Homo sapiens, had mastered.

In a recent development, homo erectus, an extinct human relative, spread from Africa across Asia. It was thought to need grassland and open woodland.

Fossil teeth from two caves in southern China suggest that Homo erectus lived in a rainforest landscape.

They are also far younger than any other firmly dated fossil of the species on the Chinese mainland.

The study was led by Kira Westaway at Macquarie University in Sydney and Renaud Joannes-Boyau at Southern Cross University. Colleagues in China and Europe also took part.

Industry observers note that only a handful of teeth were found, and their dates span a broad window. By the team’s estimate, the species was present sometime between 324,000 and 184,000 years ago.

The two caves are known as Baxian and Naxian. Both are found in Guangxi, among steep limestone hills, roughly 9 miles (15 kilometers) from each other.

At the back of each cave sits a small chamber where fossils have been cemented into rock. More than 18,000 mammal fossils have been recovered from these chambers.

Porcupines may have brought many of the fossils into the caves.

Nine of those fossils were teeth from ancient humans.

Researchers assigned eight of the nine teeth to Homo erectus based on their shape, with ancient enamel proteins supporting the identification of four.

Researchers from the Institute of Vertebrate Paleontology and Paleoanthropology in Beijing were part of the team. The institute also provided access to the excavated fossils.

Westaway’s team used five independent methods to date the teeth and the cave deposits around them.

Two of them work out when grains of sediment were last exposed to sunlight. The rest rely on uranium, which decays slowly in the teeth and in a mineral crust capping the fossils.

Industry observers note that in total, 45 ages were obtained. Forty-three of them were fed into a statistical model.

The model gave a 95% probability that Homo erectus was there sometime between 324,000 and 184,000 years ago.

Sources indicate that that span is a measure of how uncertain the dates are. It doesn’t mean the species stayed there for all 140,000 years.

The new teeth date to between 324,000 and 184,000 years ago, making them younger than the previous firmly dated finds in China, which were about 400,000 years old.

“This is a fascinating discovery because it confirms the presence of Homo erectus in a location we were not expecting and at a time we hadn’t considered,” Westaway stated.

In a recent development, elsewhere, the species hung on even longer. Fossils from the Indonesian island of Java show it there until roughly 117,000 to 108,000 years ago.

Industry observers note that what an animal eats is written into its tooth enamel as chemistry. Carbon from trees and shrubs looks different there from carbon taken in from tropical grasses.

So by testing a tooth, scientists can tell whether its owner fed in forest or in open country.

No signature of tropical grasses was found in the teeth that were tested.

Many values were low enough to indicate a dense, closed canopy. A similar pattern has been recorded in forests of the western Amazon.

Recent findings suggest that the mix of species fits this picture. Orangutans, elephants, rhinoceroses and tapirs were found among the fossils. Most of the animals were forest dwellers.

It has been revealed that other chemical tests pointed to a humid climate. Conditions were wetter and cooler than in the region today.

Three Homo erectus teeth from Naxian were then tested in the same way. Their carbon values fell in the same forest range.

Those readings fell right where dense canopy gives way to more open forest.

Nicolas Bourgon, affiliated with the Max Planck Institute of Geoanthropology in Germany, also took part in the research.

“In this case, the animal teeth and the Homo erectus teeth are telling the same story,” stated Bourgon.

Recent findings suggest that strontium is locked into enamel as well. It’s picked up from local rock by water and plants, and animals take it in when they eat and drink. Each type of rock has its own strontium signature.

Teeth form in childhood, between the ages of 2 and 6. Their strontium therefore records where a child’s food and water came from.

Strontium was measured in four Homo erectus teeth. One came from Baxian and three came from Naxian. Each tooth carried signatures from more than one kind of rock.

So each child either moved between regions, or else ate food that had been gathered from several places.

A few of those signatures were consistent with the limestone near the caves.

In a recent development, the most extreme ones best matched rock about 155 miles (250 kilometers) to the south. That area lies toward the Red River valley in northern Vietnam.

“This suggests these humans were far more mobile than previously recognized, moving across surprisingly large distances through a complex rainforest landscape,” Joannes-Boyau noted.

Still, the strontium evidence was called limited by the authors, and their reading of it tentative.

Rainforest has played a part in the debate over how Homo erectus died out.

Recent findings suggest that on Java, the last known members of the species lived in open woodland. Rainforest was expanding around them at the time.

Industry observers note that it has been proposed that the spreading forest contributed to the extinction there. In this view, the species could not adapt to it.

The teeth from Guangxi complicate that idea. Homo erectus was “not ecologically excluded from rainforest environments,” the authors wrote.

Scientists use the word hominin for humans and our extinct close relatives.

“This is the first clear, direct evidence we have for another hominin living within these habitats,” remarked Patrick Roberts, also of the Max Planck Institute of Geoanthropology.

In a recent development, the date range also overlaps with fossils of Denisovans, another extinct human group. Their remains have been found in Laos, on the Tibetan Plateau, in northeastern China and off Taiwan.

The authors wrote that several kinds of humans may have lived across the region during the same period.

In a recent development, the case for rainforest life rests on very few human teeth. Carbon values were obtained from only three of them, and all three came from one cave.

Industry observers note that the teeth show that Homo erectus could survive among rainforest animals. They cannot show that the species did well there.

The authors also wrote that rainforest may not have been its ideal habitat.

It remains unclear whether this ability was limited to late survivors in southern China. It may also have been shared by the species more widely.

To settle that question, the same enamel tests will be needed on fossils from other sites of a similar age.

The full study was published in the journal Nature.

#42829. Tech Report: A compound used by dentists helped immune cells kill bacteria hiding inside them

📅 21 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 9m • 📚 Deep Dive (1761 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Earth ↗ Open Full Page

Tech Report: A compound used by dentists helped immune cells kill bacteria hiding inside them

📅 21 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 9 min read (1761 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Earth

⏱️ ~9 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • In lab tests, K21, a compound used in a dental cleanser, helped some human immune cells kill bacteria that can survive inside them.
  • Sources indicate that white blood cells protect the body by swallowing and breaking down bacteria.
  • A newly introduced study found that K21, a chemical used in dental cleaning products, helped certain human immune cells kill more bacteria in laboratory tests.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In lab tests, K21, a compound used in a dental cleanser, helped some human immune cells kill bacteria that can survive inside them.

Sources indicate that white blood cells protect the body by swallowing and breaking down bacteria. But some bacteria survive inside these cells, making them harder to get rid of.

A newly introduced study found that K21, a chemical used in dental cleaning products, helped certain human immune cells kill more bacteria in laboratory tests.

Interestingly, the cells continued to kill more bacteria even after researchers removed K21, suggesting that the chemical had changed how the cells worked.

The researchers also found that K21 increased the breakdown and recycling of mitochondria, the tiny structures that provide energy to cells.

When they tested the chemical on small worms, the treated worms lived longer than those that received no treatment.

Christopher Rongo of the Waksman Institute of Microbiology at Rutgers University led the research.

Bhupesh Prusty of Riga Stradiņš University was a co-corresponding author, with other researchers working in Germany, Latvia, the UK and the United States.

According to recent reports, the findings are interesting, but they come from cells grown in the laboratory and experiments with worms. Nobody has yet shown that K21 can treat an infection or help people live longer.

The cells in question are macrophages. Swallowing germs, digesting them and keeping infections in check is their job.

They don’t all work the same way, though. Some are built for fighting infection, others for repairing damaged tissue.

In a recent development, could K21 change how either type behaves? That was the question.

Recent findings suggest that blood came from healthy donors. Over nine days the team grew those cells into the two types of macrophages, and a small dose of K21, 0.28 micromoles per liter, sat in some of the dishes the whole time.

In a recent development, enterococcus faecalis went in next. It lives harmlessly in the intestines, and it turns up in hospital infections.

In a recent development, that species was picked for one trait. It can survive inside a macrophage rather than being destroyed.

In a recent development, the bacteria stayed with the cells for two hours. Gentamicin, an antibiotic, then killed off whatever remained outside them.

Industry observers note that bacterial DNA inside the cells was measured first. Treated and untreated macrophages held much the same amount.

So K21 wasn’t simply making the cells swallow more bacteria.

The macrophages were broken open next, to count the bacteria still alive inside.

Recent findings suggest that whatever spilled out went onto a gel. Living germs grow into visible colonies there, which makes counting possible.

Sources indicate that the infection-fighting macrophages needed no help. Almost nothing survived in them, treated or not.

It has been revealed that but the macrophages involved in tissue repair told a different story. Untreated repair cells let more bacteria live. Where K21 had been present earlier, far fewer came through.

Rongo said the treated cells were “much more robust at killing and clearing that bacteria.”.

That was the first real clue. Whatever K21 did to those cells outlasted the chemical itself.

There are standard ways to check whether an immune cell has changed.

One is the chemical messages cells send each other. Another is the set of proteins on their surface, which marks what kind of cell it is.

The team checked both, expecting to see some obvious differences.

Industry observers note that most of it came back unchanged. Of the two messages measured, one moved: repair-focused macrophages put out less of a substance that normally calms inflammation.

The surface proteins barely changed either.

Recent findings suggest that so the repair cells had not simply been turned into the bacteria-killing type. Whatever K21 did was subtler than that.

To find what they were missing, the team read gene activity inside thousands of individual cells, one at a time.

This time, differences appeared.

It has been revealed that two groups with stronger inflammation-related activity grew more common under K21. One group of repair-focused macrophages thinned out.

Three genes caught the team’s attention: IDO1, IDO2 and KYNU.

All three help break down tryptophan, a substance we get from food. Serotonin is built from the same amino acid.

The connection was worth exploring, although the study did not show that K21 changed serotonin levels.

Measuring serotonin in animals given K21 is what the researchers want next. That would show whether the gene activity means anything inside a living body.

The team also noticed something interesting about mitochondria.

According to recent reports, they produce a cell’s energy. Like anything else in there, they wear out and need replacing.

Sources indicate that cells handle that themselves. They break mitochondria into smaller pieces and recycle the damaged ones, through a process called mitophagy.

The researchers wondered whether K21 was affecting this cleanup system.

Macrophage mitochondria are hard to examine closely, so two other types of human cell took the imaging.

In both, K21 left the mitochondria more broken up. Signs of recycling grew stronger too.

Other chemicals push cells into recycling their mitochondria. K21 was not working the same way.

In a recent development, it increased a protein called Drp1, which helps mitochondria split into smaller pieces. Similar activity turned up in the macrophages, though only in the cells associated with tissue repair.

That was especially interesting because these were the same cells that had become better at killing bacteria.

Sources indicate that could changing how mitochondria are maintained help explain the stronger response to bacteria? The results point in that direction, but they don’t yet prove how the two changes are connected.

According to recent reports, rongo’s laboratory already works on mitochondria and on how animals cope when oxygen runs low. That gave the researchers another way to investigate K21.

They turned to Caenorhabditis elegans, tiny, transparent worms that scientists often use to study basic processes inside living cells.

The team added K21 to the worms’ food and watched what happened.

Sources indicate that the worms did what the human cells had done. More breaking down and recycling of mitochondria, and the mitochondria themselves came out shorter and rounder.

Sources indicate that worms missing certain genes for that process were tested too. In those animals nothing changed.

That suggested K21 depended on the worms’ normal machinery for dividing and recycling mitochondria.

Recent findings suggest that the researchers then asked a different question. Would any of this affect how long the worms lived?

They followed 151 worms given K21 and compared them with 128 untreated worms across three experiments.

The difference was clear. Worms that received K21 lived significantly longer.

But there was something the team needed to rule out first.

In a recent development, A worm on short rations lives longer, which has been known for years. Reduced feeding would have been the dull explanation.

The researchers checked, and the opposite happened. Worms given K21 actually fed a little faster.

The chemical also did not appear to affect their growth, body size, reproduction or ability to survive through development.

Sources indicate that there were many changes happening inside their cells, though. K21 increased the activity of 1,848 genes and reduced the activity of another 1,312.

Even so, Rongo warned against reading too much into the lifespan result. Helping a tiny worm live longer is very different from helping a person live longer.

There are still some key gaps in the research.

Recent findings suggest that the immune cell changes indicated up only in cultures holding a mixture of cell types. Take the mixture away and the effect went with it.

Much of the detailed work on mitochondria also took place in cells that weren’t macrophages.

The researchers used HUVEC cells, which come from the lining of blood vessels, and U2-OS cells, which come from a bone cancer cell line.

The bacterial experiments were limited too. The team tested one bacterial species, using one K21 pretreatment schedule, with three replicates.

They did not give K21 to an infected animal or test whether it helped a human wound heal.

It has been revealed that there was a reason wound healing had attracted their attention in the first place. Earlier research by Gulve and colleagues, beginning in 2016, had reported faster wound healing in animals.

Those findings helped lead the team toward the immune cells examined in this study.

Industry observers note that the worms bring another problem when thinking about human health. They don’t have macrophages at all, and roughly a billion years of evolution separate them from people.

It has been revealed that so the worm experiments can tell scientists something about basic cell processes. They cannot tell us whether K21 would have the same benefits in humans.

The researchers also disclosed where their funding came from.

According to recent reports, part of the work was supported by the National Institutes of Health. The remaining support came from FiteBac, the organization that markets K21.

FiteBac also supplied the material used in the worm experiments.

Industry observers note that rongo has no ownership stake in the organization and no patent on K21, although he received a pilot grant from FiteBac. Prusty received a research grant.

Industry observers note that these details matter because the manufacturer has a commercial interest in the compound. Independent studies would help establish whether the findings can be repeated.

Even after all these experiments, the team still doesn’t know exactly what K21 attaches to inside a cell.

Its chemical structure offers one possible explanation.

K21 has four fatty acid chains attached to a central structure known as quaternary ammonium silane. Together, these give the compound properties that might allow it to collect in the fatty membranes surrounding mitochondria.

The researchers suspect that could help explain what they observed.

But they have not identified a specific molecule that K21 binds to, so the idea remains unproven.

Industry observers note that the researchers now want to test K21 in living animals. They initiative to measure serotonin levels to see whether the gene changes found in cells also matter in the body.

They could also give K21 to infected animals and check how many bacteria survive. This would help show whether the compound can fight infections outside the lab.

It has been revealed that so far, K21 has helped human immune cells kill more bacteria and made tiny worms live longer. Whether it can benefit people remains unknown.

The study is published in the journal Life Science Alliance.

Bipartisan process for picking GAO chief breaks down

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Sources indicate that chairman Rand Paul, R-Ky., speaks during a Senate Homeland Security and Governmental Affairs Committee business meeting on Sept.
  • Republican leaders have skipped a bipartisan deliberative process for recommending the next comptroller general to head the Government Accountability Office, as lawmakers prepare to consider a nomination for the post from President Donald Trump.
  • Industry observers note that sources stated Trump is planning to nominate Eric Ueland, who right now serves as deputy director for management at the Office of Management and Budget.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Sources indicate that chairman Rand Paul, R-Ky., speaks during a Senate Homeland Security and Governmental Affairs Committee business meeting on Sept. 23. (Tom Williams/CQ Roll Call).

Republican leaders have skipped a bipartisan deliberative process for recommending the next comptroller general to head the Government Accountability Office, as lawmakers prepare to consider a nomination for the post from President Donald Trump.

Industry observers note that sources stated Trump is planning to nominate Eric Ueland, who right now serves as deputy director for management at the Office of Management and Budget. The White House submitted ethics paperwork on Ueland — required for nominations — to the GAO, according to a source.

Recent findings suggest that senate Homeland Security and Governmental Affairs Chairman Rand Paul, R-Ky., on Thursday posted notice of a committee hearing Nov. 19 to examine more than a dozen presidential nominees for executive and judicial offices, including “a nominee to be Comptroller General.”.

The post identifies by name all of the nominees except the candidate for comptroller general. The post has been filled by an acting comptroller general, Orice Williams Brown, since Gene L. Dodaro completed his 15-year term at the end of last year.

Sources indicate that the move by Paul to short-circuit the convening of a legislative commission to recommend candidates infuriated top Democrats, who excoriated the chairman in a joint statement Wednesday night. A special bipartisan, bicameral legislative commission is supposed to recommend at least three candidates for comptroller general to the president, according to statute.

It has been revealed that homeland Security Committee GOP staff solicited recommendations for a comptroller general from some Democratic congressional offices Wednesday afternoon, imposing a deadline of 8 a.m. Thursday, according to Democratic aides.

The president nominates the head of the GAO, the investigative arm of Congress, with the advice and consent of the Senate.

According to recent reports, paul pushed back on the criticism Thursday, saying, “Democrats have known about this for months and months and months.” He said the last time the special commission made recommendations for the office, when Barack Obama was president, “Democrats submitted their own list, Republicans submitted their own list. So they can complain all they want but they just need to make their list and submit it.”.

In the past, however, the special commission convened, sought applications for the position, interviewed candidates and deliberated before sending recommendations to the president.

A 1980 law states that when there is a vacancy in the comptroller general position, “there is established a commission to recommend individuals to the President for appointment to the vacant office,” and that the commission must submit at least three names.

Under the statute, the commission includes the speaker, Senate majority and minority leaders, House majority and minority leaders, chairs and ranking members of the Senate Homeland Security and House Oversight and Government Reform committees, and the Senate president pro tempore.

Industry observers note that in 1981, for example, after the law took effect, the two congressional leaders, Speaker Thomas P. “Tip” O’Neill Jr., D-Mass., and Senate Majority Leader Howard H. Baker, R-Tenn., sent a letter to President Ronald Reagan saying the special commission had met and voted to recommend eight candidates to succeed Comptroller General Elmer Staats.

“The members of the Commission have taken their statutory responsibility seriously,” they wrote.

Reagan nominated Charles A. Bowsher, who was on the list, and he was confirmed.

After Bowsher’s term ended in 1996, the commission eventually formed, interviewed multiple candidates, and deliberated for several months. Republicans controlled both chambers, and Bill Clinton was president. The members of the commission could not reach agreement, and as a result, the Republicans on the committee submitted their list to Clinton, and the Democrats on the panel submitted theirs.

Clinton also had his own list. Clinton nominated David M. Walker, who was on all three lists, and he was confirmed by the Senate more than two years after Bowsher’s departure. Walker argued Thursday against short-circuiting the commission process.

“The position is of critical importance and the related statutory Commission process should not be circumvented," Walker noted. "Doing so would undercut the credibility of the person and the effectiveness of the GAO.”.

Walker resigned in March of 2008, when George W. Bush was still president. He appointed Dodaro as acting comptroller general when he left. The commission got going several months later, creating a website with application instructions and candidate questions.

Sources indicate that over the next two years, the commission interviewed some 20 candidates. Democrats and Republicans on the panel were unable to reach agreement, and Democrats, who had a majority on the commission, submitted their own list to Obama in 2010. Republicans followed up with their list.

“The Commission has been working in earnest on this undertaking for more than one year and has dedicated considerable time and effort to present you with highly qualified candidates for this important position,” then-Speaker Nancy Pelosi, D-Calif., and then-Senate Majority Leader Harry Reid, D-Nev., along with other Democratic leaders, wrote to Obama when they submitted the Democrats’ list.

The Democrats’ move drew a rebuke from Sen. Susan Collins, R-Maine, who was ranking member of the Senate Homeland Security and Governmental Affairs Committee at the time.

Industry observers note that collins stated in a statement she was “extremely disappointed” that Democrats “abruptly ended the selection process for the next Comptroller General without a bipartisan agreement” on the recommendations. “We have had several exceptionally qualified individuals apply to be the next leader of the GAO, and it should have been possible to come up with a consensus list.”.

Obama nominated and the Senate confirmed Dodaro, who was one of four recommendations from the Democrats.

The 8 Best Solar Generators Provide Reliable Backup Power in a Pinch

📅 13 Aug 2021 | ⏱️ 17 min read (3455 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Popularmechanics

⏱️ ~17 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Gear-obsessed editors choose every product we review.
  • In a recent development, power stations (i.e., solar generators) have become increasingly popular because they are easy to run, cost less over time than gas generators, and offer eco-friendly, emission-free operation, especially when paired with a solar panel.
  • Unlike fuel-based generators, solar generators can’t create electricity in real time.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Gear-obsessed editors choose every product we review. We may earn commission if you buy from a link. Why Trust Us?

In a recent development, power stations (i.e., solar generators) have become increasingly popular because they are easy to run, cost less over time than gas generators, and offer eco-friendly, emission-free operation, especially when paired with a solar panel. Some are small and compact, ideal for off-grid adventures, while larger ones are able to back up critical home circuits during a blackout.

Unlike fuel-based generators, solar generators can’t create electricity in real time. They’re giant battery packs, not true generators, and need to be recharged using alternating current (AC) power or solar panels, the latter of which often takes many hours in ideally sunny conditions.

Despite those distinctions compared to portable generators, there’s nothing more convenient than a power station for charging or running everything you need for day-to-day life—phones and laptops, lights, and even a small appliance or two. Plus, it’s nice to have a device that doesn’t produce carbon emissions and replenishes itself freely from the sun’s rays. Whether you’re seeking a highly portable option or need one that’s heavy-duty enough for extended use, these are the best solar generators we’ve tested and researched to date.

In a recent development, to pick the best solar generators, we tested some of these power stations for charging capacity, ease of use, weight, and different use cases. Our picks were reviewed by Popular Mechanics editor Brad Ford, who provided input for the larger-capacity units. Other models on this list were reviewed by test editor David Dritsas or freelance writer Maggie Slepian.

Our primary concerns were portability and convenience. Ease of use was also important—was the display easy to read? Did the screen readouts make sense? Bonus points if we could tell how much power is available at a glance. In the past few years, these criteria have become easier to meet. There are now plenty of compact, affordable units that have better charging capabilities than before.

Very few power stations of this size can handle as much solar input power as the Bluetti Apex 200. With two input types—low-voltage XT60 (up to 1,000 watts) and high-voltage MC4 (up to 2,000 watts)—it can accept up to 3,000 watts of solar power. If you had the panels and ideal weather, you could fully charge this station in less than 2 hours—even faster than plugging it into the wall. That’s impressive.

In a recent development, it also balances nicely between being a portable station and a home backup solution. It offers 3,200 watts of continuous power (it notes 3,600 on the front, but that’s only if it’s connected to an expansion battery). We were able to power a refrigerator for a full 27 hours on a single charge, and estimated the battery efficiency at 90 percent, which is very good. Meanwhile, the 2,560-watt-hour battery capacity is expandable by adding up to six additional batteries. Using Bluetti’s largest battery, the B500K, you could build a massive 33-kilowatt-hour system.

While 3,600 watts isn’t enough to power a whole home, you could power a couple of circuits through a manual transfer switch using the 120-volt 30-amp output. But keep in mind that there’s no 240-volt support, so you can’t use it to power high-voltage appliances like electric dryers.

As a portable station, the Apex 200 has a lot to offer. At 59 pounds, it’s not too hard to move around the house or in and out of a vehicle. And there are several great DC power options, including a bank of USB outlets (two are high-power USB-C) and both 10- and 30-amp, 12-volt outputs. We also love that the AC ports can individually be turned on and off using the mobile app; this helps improve overall runtime.

Since very few stations can match its max solar input capacity, we concluded that the Apex 200 is definitely a top choice for anyone who wants a power station that can recharge using the sun’s rays, but also offers the versatility of being used on the road or at home.

Full Bluetti Apex 200 Power Station Review.

Industry observers note that this model replaces the original Jackery 1000, but many of the same observations made of the first model still apply. The fresh version has a slightly higher capacity of 1,070 watt-hours and uses a newer lithium iron phosphate (LiFePO4) battery, which is a newer battery technology that offers a longer lifespan (4,000 cycles versus 500 cycles for this model) and better performance in extreme temperatures.

Expert Maggie Slepian used the previous model on a media trip where she had to keep multiple camera batteries charged during a weeklong outing. She found that while the capacity was lower than you'll find with others on this list, it actually powers items for longer than some higher-capacity models. She also charged her photographer’s camera batteries while charging the power bank on solar power (it was a very sunny winter day), which proved effective and efficient.

The newer V2 model has seven ports, including three AC outlets, two USB-C ports (one 30-watt and one 100-watt), a 12-volt car port, and one standard 18-watt USB-A outlet. It charges a typical laptop eight times or powers a small refrigerator or an electric cooler for over 15 hours.

According to recent reports, the Jackery Explorer 1000 V2 charges with a 200-watt solar panel or a 12-volt outlet in your vehicle while you’re on the move. It has fairly standard charging times, with 11.5 hours in a car outlet, 6.5 hours for solar panels, and just 5.5 hours to fully charge in a wall outlet. This won’t be your best bet for powering larger appliances, but it’s an ideal power station for smaller items and off-grid camping.

According to recent reports, the EcoFlow Delta Pro is a large portable power station with an output that rivals some gas portable generators. When sold in a bundle with solar panels, like the package with two 220-watt portable panels we tested, it becomes a powerful solar generator. With an output of 3,600 watts, the Delta Pro can charge multiple appliances, and the output has the ability to bump up to 4,500 watts with its built-in X-Boost technology if more power is needed.

Industry observers note that to get an idea of the run time, we used the Delta Pro to power a full-size, 25-cubic-foot refrigerator—which it did for a remarkable 51 hours and 24 minutes. When recharged from a standard outlet, it took only two hours and 36 minutes. But it also charges with the included adapter, at electric vehicle charging stations, with a DC car adapter, or with the solar panels that come with the unit. Through the 30-amp connection, you can also connect this to a transfer switch to directly power select circuits in your home.

In a recent development, like any power station with a large battery capacity, it will take a long time, perhaps nearly two days, to recharge this station using the bundled 220-watt solar panels. The good news is the Delta Pro accepts up to 1,600 watts of solar input, so it can charge faster by connecting more panels.

The heavy-duty wheels and telescoping handle on Anker’s Solix F3000 are easy to use, allow you to stand upright when pulling, and are a dream for people who regularly find themselves moving their power station around, whether it’s at a campsite or to different parts of the house during a power outage.

Along with convenience, this generator is a powerhouse with the capacity to easily run your refrigerator or a greenhouse heater, or keep your RV bright and warm.

We were impressed with Anker’s app, which allows us to check the charging status or power being generated without continually going outside to check. The app also lets you turn the power to the AC and USB ports on and off remotely, keeping tabs on how much energy is being utilized.

The Solix F3000 has 11 ports, including two car ports, an RV-specific outlet, four AC ports, three USB-C charging ports, and two USB-A. In sunny conditions and moderate temperatures, it recharges with a 400-watt solar panel in just a few hours and supports up to 2,400 watts of solar input.

One of Jackery’s most recent solar generators is also its most rugged, able to withstand the elements better than most. It achieves this with an IP65 weatherproof rating, molded rubber port covers, a shockproof enclosure, and a bottom drainage system, which is part of a titanium alloy cooling structure that helps keep water out of the enclosure.

Industry observers note that we got a chance to see these features up close and were impressed by them all, as well as a very sturdy enclosure that, thanks to the cooling system design, eliminates any side vents that could allow water to get inside. It feels strong; you could bang this station around without worrying too much about damaging it. The only downside is that this denser construction adds a bit of weight.

As a power station, it delivers 1,800 watts of output with a battery capacity of 1,536 watt-hours. That’s enough power for a weekend camping trip or for running low-powered small appliances and some lighting during an emergency. As a solar generator, it can handle up to 800 watts of input from a portable panel. We paired it with a Jackery 200-watt panel, and it worked well. Overall, if your off-road adventures often get a little dirty, but you need some extra power, the Jackery Explorer 1500 Ultra Power Station is a good one to have at your side.

Full Jackery Explorer 1500 Ultra Power Station Review.

In a recent development, the latest version of the Goal Zero Yeti 1500 is a well-designed power station that’s ideal for off-grid camping situations where dust, wind, and potentially wet conditions are always on the table. This 2,000-watt power station is weatherproof with an IPX4 rating and features outlet shields that cover the ports and inputs. Each section is well-lit by an LED light that’s individually turned on or off using a manual button or the mobile app (and will shut off if not used after a certain period).

There’s a healthy number of outputs on the Yeti 1500, including four 120-volt AC outlets, four (two are high-powered) USB-A ports, and four 12-volt connections. We simulated an emergency blackout and managed to run a cable modem with a WiFi router, a lamp, a TV, and a tower fan, while charging a phone and a laptop through the USB-C ports. Given the station’s output and capacity, there was enough power for over two days of use (conveniently shown on the main display), and there was plenty of room to spare for a few more devices.

To test its solar capabilities, we paired the Yeti 1500 with a Nomad 200-watt portable solar panel and connected it using the high-voltage DC input, which accepts up to 600 watts; however, it also features a low-voltage input that accepts up to 300 watts for smaller panel arrays. Because both inputs can be used simultaneously, you could theoretically pair with two arrays for up to 900 watts, which is a high amount of input for a station of this size.

Industry observers note that of course, no portable panel operates at 100 percent efficiency. Even on a sunny, cloudless day with no shade-causing obstructions, the input readings demonstrated anywhere from 125 to 145 watts. After initiating a recharge with only 5 percent capacity left, it would take at least 10.5 hours in those conditions to recharge. That’s actually not bad. An average of about 70 percent efficiency for a portable panel is good.

Full Goal Zero Yeti 1500 Review.

Sources indicate that this power station takes solar recharging seriously. The Elite 300 can accept up to 1,200 watts of input, which is a high amount for a station this size. We paired it with a 250-watt portable panel and, on a fully sunny day, got around 260 watts of input. That’s the typical efficiency of a portable panel (again, you’ll never get 100 percent). But pair it with some larger panels, and you’ll get even more.

It also boasts an impressive battery capacity of just over 3,000 watt-hours and 2,400 watts of output, which is high for a station of this size. Plus, it includes a 120-volt 30-amp port, which is handy for connecting it to a small RV or pop-up camper, allowing you to run small appliances and water pumps. It’s not enough power to run a heating or cooling system for a significant amount of time, but for lights, small appliances, and other items that need power, this station will deliver.

If there’s one downside we found, it’s that there’s no way to add an expansion battery to increase your capacity. That’s not a huge detractor, but it’s something we’ve seen in stations even smaller than this one. But at the end of the day, the Bluetti Elite 300 solar generator offers the right balance between a midsize power station that delivers a lot of power and run time, and a station that is compact and portable enough to be perfectly suited for an outdoor adventure.

Full Bluetti Elite 300 Solar Generator Review.

The Anker Solix C2000 power station can deliver the full 2,400 watts of output to the bank of five AC outlets—something similar stations don’t offer. This allows you to power several things at once, like a refrigerator, toaster, router, and chargers, all at the same time.

During our tests, we were able to take full advantage of this, powering a refrigerator (by itself for up to 18 hours), along with some high-powered appliances, like a four-slot toaster and an electric kettle (though not the last two at the same time).

Another interesting ability of the C2000 is that you can fast charge it from AC power up to 1,800 watts, but that recharging rate remains consistent if you’re powering other devices at the same time (we confirmed this with a wattmeter). For example, we ran a 1,400-watt space heater while still recharging at the full 1,800-watt rate. Other power stations offer similar fast charging but will throttle the amount of power coming into the station while powering devices.

Sources indicate that for solar recharging, we were a bit disappointed that this station can only accept 800 watts of input; other stations of this size accept more. But when solar was plugged in, it worked well. We connected it to a 200-watt Anker portable panel, and in full sun, we were getting around 125 to 145 watts of input, which is pretty good as these types of panels go. The C2000 is not IPX-rated for any type of weather resistance, however, so we would not recommend leaving this station sitting outside if the weather turns wet.

Full Anker Solix C2000 Power Station Review.

It has been revealed that power stations use watts and watt-hours to express size and capacity. Watts (size) refer to how much power it produces. For example, if you need to run a 900-watt microwave, you’ll need a station that outputs at least that much power (ideally more, since factory specs are never exact).

Meanwhile, watt-hours (capacity) give you an idea of how long devices can be powered continuously, though how much time depends on the amount of power being drawn—watt-hours don’t dictate a set time frame. Higher-powered devices will drain the battery a lot faster than lower-powered ones.

That may seem confusing, but a simple equation gives you an approximate idea of how it works: total watt-hours (of the generator) ÷ watts (of the device) = hours the power station runs.

For example, if you had a power station with a 2,048-watt-hour capacity and wanted to run a 750-watt space heater consistently at its highest setting, it would probably run for around 2.5 hours, so long as nothing else is plugged in. But for a refrigerator, whose power draw fluctuates between 10 and 300 watts (depending on how often the compressor turns on), you might be able to run it for nearly 24 hours.

Keep in mind that manufacturer specs are taken from perfect conditions; in the real world, you’ll likely see slightly less capacity from your power station. If you’re not sure how much power the different devices in your home draw, sometimes it’s written on a label, or you can use a device like a wattmeter.

Just as a power station has specifications on output size and capacity, solar panels are rated by how many watts they produce for a device after they convert the sun’s rays into electrical current (e.g., 100 watts, 200 watts, etc.). Because real-world conditions are never perfect, it’s not uncommon for panels to only output 50 to 75 percent (or even lower) of their total potential.

Recent findings suggest that your panels must also be within the acceptable input range of the power station. For example, connecting a 400-watt solar-panel array to a power station that only accepts 110 watts of solar input can cause an overload and damage the station.

In a recent development, while weight and size don’t directly correlate to the technicalities of power banks, they impact the convenience of each model. Many camping and overlanding setups have limited space, so the more compact models likely have a higher appeal as a result.

That noted, most units weigh at least 10 pounds, and the weight and size increase promptly with greater capacities. Before purchasing, consider where you proposal to store the power bank and the space in your vehicle or camper where it will live while you’re on the road. If you plan to use this power bank solely as a home backup option, portability will matter less, but consider how much effort it will take to move it around within your home or in your outdoor space.

Recent findings suggest that I am a low-maintenance camper, and most of my background is in lightweight backcountry travel. That means I prioritize space-saving and ease-of-use, so my go-to power banks have between 250 and 600 watt-hours, and weigh less than 15 pounds.

This is perfect for a weekend trip, with the on-the-go (car or solar) charging capabilities to put my mind at ease for longer trips. Mostly, I’m charging small items, so one charge lasts a long time. However, plenty of people in the van-life and remote-work world are powering their RVs and vans, and relying on multiple laptop charges. For that, I’d recommend one of the larger units.

In a recent development, A solar-powered generator charges and runs almost anything that requires power—it just depends on the capacity. These generators can charge power tools in the shop, laptops for remote work, and personal devices like Bluetooth headphones and speakers.

A solar-powered generator with a higher power capacity can even power household appliances in the event of a power outage. And the fact that these are solar-compatible means you aren’t reliant on the electrical grid to recharge them.

Every unit on our list has multiple charging options, including wall (AC outlet), car (12-volt), and solar. Each input method charges your unit at a different speed, and solar also depends on the conditions. AC power is the fastest, followed by 12-volt, and then by solar (though a larger solar array could potentially be faster than 12-volt).

I try to charge up my power banks whenever I can, so I’m never caught off guard trying to leave on a trip with a dying power bank. If this happens (which it has), I’ll charge it in my vehicle’s 12-volt port while I’m driving, though this is often slower than solar or a wall unit.

In a recent development, solar power is the most sustainable and typically fastest way to power these—just be sure you have enough wattage in the solar panels to make it effective. I recommend keeping the generator stored with at least an 80 percent charge, and unplugging it once it’s fully charged—keeping it plugged in longer than necessary degrades the battery.

Most units will have a simple readout display showing the remaining battery charge, and it’s a good practice not to allow your battery pack to get below 20 percent.

It has been revealed that asteroid 6993 (1995 BJ4), a small body 7 miles (11 kilometers) across, orbits in the main belt between Mars and Jupiter. In August 2026, astronomers spotted a faint tail, making it candidate for the largest known main-belt comet. However, the tail has been gradually fading through 2026, which hints at it being caused by debris from a one-time impact rather than ongoing outgassing, astronomers reported last month in a paper accepted in The Astrophysical Journal Letters.
